# text = The Internet occasionally reminds me of how different life is because of it .

# text = I noted on Facebook that , from a statistical perspective , what makes baseball such an amazing sport is that you can watch it your entire life and still see , on a daily basis , something you RSQUOve never seen before .
# text = In this case , the something in question was watching the wonderfully named Angel Pagan hit an inside - the - park home run and initiate a triple play in the same game .

# text = John Emerson responded with some humbug about it not being an inside - the - park grand slam , which made me remember that I had seen an inside - the - park grand slam at some time in the remote past .
# text = The fact that I can verify vague memories of events that occurred twenty - five years ago astounds me in a way I sometimes forget the Internet is capable of doing .

# text = This realization is obviously not of world - historical importance , merely a reminder that this thing whose existence we take for granted daily represents a fundamentally weird complement to human memory .

# text = This post is the first of a three - part series on bike culture .
# text = Come back Friday to read about anarchy , bike jousting , and two - wheeled social protest .
# text = Remember when you got your first bike ?
# text = Was it a Christmas present , or maybe a birthday gift ?
# text = Remember how much fun you used to have on that bike , how fast you went , how great it felt ?
# text = Well , these days , most kids want an Xbox for their birthday ; their parents ride around in cars with seatbelts , talking on their phones .
# text = Cycling is a thing of the past : a sport , a hobby , but rarely a mode of transportation .
# text = But I 'm here to tell you : riding your bike is still fun , and still fast , and it 's the cheapest and most socially responsible workout you 'll ever get .
# text = And there are no two ways about it : if you give a kid a bike , that kid will ride .
# text = In Troy , New York , I met one Andrew Lynn .
# text = He 's somewhat of a man brain trust , and one of his best creations is the Troy Bike Rescue .
# text = It started in 2001 , when Andrew would ride around town pulling bikes out of dumpsters .
# text = He started hosting work parties with friends in his backyard , teaching them to fix their bikes and helping them get started riding .
# text = Slowly but surely , the circle grew and Andrew 's backyard parties became weekly workshops .
# text = When Andrew decided to leave town for a few years ' schooling in NYC , friends and cohorts took over operations .
# text = These days it 's an established club , run by volunteers and donations , turning trashed bikes into treasures .
# text = TBR 's customers run the gamut , from businessmen to street kids to college students to families .
# text = The one thing they have in common ?
# text = This group understands the value of a bicycle : more than just transportation , a bike is a statement against fossil fuels .
# text = More than a toy , it 's an equalizer that allows poor kids to ride with rich .
# text = More than a hobby , it 's a way of traveling through the world that lets you interact , use your muscles , breathe fresh air -- all for the cost of a free dumpster bike .
# text = TBR hosts workshops twice a week .
# text = For a few hours , the doors are open to anyone who walks in .
# text = Tools are available , and volunteers will help with advice and knowledge .
# text = Parts can be had for a pittance , and you can pick out your own bike from the stacks and racks of machines filling the space .
# text = The main focus of TBR , however , is not selling bikes .
# text = The idea is to give people a workspace and teach them how to maintain their own bicycle .
# text = Self - sufficiency is a major tenet of the bike movement , and Troy Bike Rescue is training self - reliant individuals of all stripes .
# text = All around me , college students and bike punks tinkered with their machines .
# text = An older man asked for tips on tuning his racer .
# text = A dad came in with his three kids , all of whom left with snazzy rides -- but first , they all sat down and worked on their new wheels together .
# text = And as we left at the end of the workshop , a woman walked up to Andrew .
# text = " I love what you do , " she said .
# text = " I have a whole bunch of bikes to give you . "
# text = See , ultimately TBR is about more than just bicycles .
# text = It 's about building community , and triggering a quiet but inexorable social movement .
# text = This is not the world 's first bike collective ; in fact it 's only one of many that have stealthily sprung up around America .
# text = These collectives are not waiting for change to happen : they 're creating it through small , positive , peaceful actions .
# text = You too can change the world : all you have to do is ride a bike .
# text = Try This at Home : Ride Around
# text = What are you waiting for ?
# text = Bikes are cheap : you can get one at your local thrift store for $ 5 - 50 .
# text = It does n't have to be perfect , just good enough to get you places .
# text = So pick one up , and ride it to the end of your block !
# text = Even if your life requires four wheels , you can use a bike for local errands .
# text = Ride it to the corner store when you need milk , instead of driving across town to the grocery store .
# text = Tell the store owner what you like , and see if he 'll carry it .
# text = On weekends , instead of driving to the park , hop on your bike and go exploring .
# text = It does n't have to be a workout : you can just toodle around town and look at stuff .
# text = Or , if you 're a gym buff , trade a workout for a bike ride .
# text = Unless you live on a major highway , odds are you can ride straight from your front porch to someplace interesting .
# text = It 's cheaper , and much better for the local flora & fauna .
# text = Then think of it this way : by riding your bike instead of driving your car , you 're reducing your consumption of fossil fuels .
# text = You can even calculate the money you save on gas , and keep it in a jar for a rainy day .
# text = Bike clubs tend to be pretty anarchic , but if you look around your community you 'll find both bike riders and shop owners who ride for change .

# text = Remember when you got your first bike ?
# text = Was it a Christmas present , or maybe a birthday gift ?
# text = Remember how much fun you used to have on that bike , how fast you went , how great it felt ?
# text = Well , these days , most kids want an Xbox for their birthday ; their parents ride around in cars with seatbelts , talking on their phones .
# text = Cycling is a thing of the past : a sport , a hobby , but rarely a mode of transportation .
# text = But I 'm here to tell you : riding your bike is still fun , and still fast , and it 's the cheapest and most socially responsible workout you 'll ever get .
# text = And there are no two ways about it : if you give a kid a bike , that kid will ride .
# text = In Troy , New York , I met one Andrew Lynn .
# text = He 's somewhat of a man brain trust , and one of his best creations is the Troy Bike Rescue .
# text = It started in 2001 , when Andrew would ride around town pulling bikes out of dumpsters .
# text = He started hosting work parties with friends in his backyard , teaching them to fix their bikes and helping them get started riding .
# text = Slowly but surely , the circle grew and Andrew 's backyard parties became weekly workshops .
# text = When Andrew decided to leave town for a few years ' schooling in NYC , friends and cohorts took over operations .
# text = These days it 's an established club , run by volunteers and donations , turning trashed bikes into treasures .
# text = TBR 's customers run the gamut , from businessmen to street kids to college students to families .
# text = The one thing they have in common ?
# text = This group understands the value of a bicycle : more than just transportation , a bike is a statement against fossil fuels .
# text = More than a toy , it 's an equalizer that allows poor kids to ride with rich .
# text = More than a hobby , it 's a way of traveling through the world that lets you interact , use your muscles , breathe fresh air -- all for the cost of a free dumpster bike .
# text = TBR hosts workshops twice a week .
# text = For a few hours , the doors are open to anyone who walks in .
# text = Tools are available , and volunteers will help with advice and knowledge .
# text = Parts can be had for a pittance , and you can pick out your own bike from the stacks and racks of machines filling the space .
# text = The main focus of TBR , however , is not selling bikes .
# text = The idea is to give people a workspace and teach them how to maintain their own bicycle .
# text = Self - sufficiency is a major tenet of the bike movement , and Troy Bike Rescue is training self - reliant individuals of all stripes .
# text = All around me , college students and bike punks tinkered with their machines .
# text = An older man asked for tips on tuning his racer .
# text = A dad came in with his three kids , all of whom left with snazzy rides -- but first , they all sat down and worked on their new wheels together .
# text = And as we left at the end of the workshop , a woman walked up to Andrew .
# text = " I love what you do , " she said .
# text = " I have a whole bunch of bikes to give you . "
# text = See , ultimately TBR is about more than just bicycles .
# text = It 's about building community , and triggering a quiet but inexorable social movement .
# text = This is not the world 's first bike collective ; in fact it 's only one of many that have stealthily sprung up around America .
# text = These collectives are not waiting for change to happen : they 're creating it through small , positive , peaceful actions .
# text = You too can change the world : all you have to do is ride a bike .

# text = Ride it to the corner store when you need milk , instead of driving across town to the grocery store .
# text = Tell the store owner what you like , and see if he 'll carry it .
# text = On weekends , instead of driving to the park , hop on your bike and go exploring .
# text = It does n't have to be a workout : you can just toodle around town and look at stuff .

# text = Jet Lag : Pathophysiology and Cures
# text = The longest Monday of my life
# text = I recently returned to the US from Australia .
# text = The 14 - hour flight took me from Monday morning in Sydney to Monday morning , again , in L.A .
# text = Crossing the date line messed up my sense of time enough without the added bonus of thinking I should be heading to bed just as the sun began to climb into the California sky .
# text = You may be familiar with the concept : Jet lag .
# text = The catch - all name for circadian misalignment , the disruption of sleep cycles and circadian rhythms .

# text = If you 've had the pleasure of crossing time zones in a jet plane , whether it was a mere three - hour hop from one coast of the US to the other or a trip to another continent , chances are , you 've experienced some amount of jet lag .
# text = The pathophysiology of jet lag
# text = Normally , two systems -- the homeostatic system and the circadian system -- work together to produce a 24 - hour sleep cycle .
# text = During the day , the homeostatic system slowly accumulates a ' sleep drive , ' a desire to sleep that increases as a function of time spent awake .
# text = The circadian system generates an alerting signal in opposition to this sleep drive , which , during the day , keeps a person from feeling increasingly sleepy .
# text = An hour or two before bedtime , this signal subsides , and s$$he realizes it 's time to hit the pillow .
# text = So we 've got a nice cycle of sleep .
# text = Jet lag is what happens when the homeostatic and circadian processes are misaligned .

# text = For example , the circadian system may signal a person to be alert when it 's not actually morning , or may be reduced during daytime hours , causing daytime sleepiness because the homeostatic sleep drive is no longer cancelled out .
# text = But I do n't want to be sleepy !
# text = How do you beat jet lag ?
# text = Robert Sack lists three primary approaches : Reset the body clock Prescribed sleep scheduling Medication to counteract daytime sleepiness or insomnia
# text = Let 's start with the first one , as it turns out to be the most complicated .
# text = The two most effective ways to reset the body clock are 1-RRB- through bright light exposure , and 2-RRB- timed melatonin administration .
# text = Studies have shown that without light cues , totally blind people tend to have free - running circadian rhythms with an average period of 24.5 hours , instead of the usual 24 .

# text = If a person is exposed to bright light early in the day , the person 's internal clock is reset to an earlier time ; if exposure is instead in the evening , the internal clock is reset to a later time .
# text = Artificial light sources can be used to supplement daylight , to help reset a person 's internal clock to the correct new time zone when traveling .
# text = Alternatively , a person could wear very dark glasses , as light avoidance could help minimize the problems of light exposure at the wrong time of day or night .
# text = Resetting the body clock , Part 2 : Melatonin
# text = Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland at night ; secretion is suppressed by light exposure , and as such , the hormone can be thought of as a " darkness signal . "
# text = If doses of melatonin are administered in the morning , circadian rhythms will be shifted later ; evening doses shift rhythms earlier .

# text = Timing of the doses is more important than amount per dose , though it remains to be seen what the optimal dose and optimal time of administration is -- trials have been done with doses from 0.5 to 10 mg , at times ranging from three days before departure to five days after arrival in the new time zone .
# text = The second way to beat jet lag : Sleep at weird times .
# text = Slowly adjust your sleep schedule to match that of your destination , or keep your home sleep schedule for a while after you arrive .

# text = The problem with this is that your sleep - wake schedule wo n't match up with that of the people around you , and if you need to be awake for breakfast at 7 am or for a meeting in the afternoon , your sleep schedule may interfere .
# text = Use this method at your own risk .
# text = Lastly , we have sleep medicines .
# text = As you might guess , hypnotic medications combat insomnia and stimulants fight off daytime sleepiness pretty well , because by definition , that 's what they do .

# text = In the study linked , subjects were treated with slow - release caffeine or with melatonin prior to a long eastward flight ; the caffeine subjects were less sleepy than either melatonin or placebo .
# text = Granted , caffeine subjects also took longer to fall asleep later and awoke more frequently , but that may be a risk you have to take .
# text = Light , melatonin , drugs , strange sleep schedules .
# text = Of course , the only solution that will always work is time .
# text = The homeostatic and circadian processes need to realign , and while the aforementioned ways of beating jet lag can fast track the process , it still takes time .
# text = UPDATE : ; I was alerted by a friend of the existence further research of which I was unaware : Another way to reset your sleep - wake cycle is to stop eating .
# text = If you fast for about 12 to 16 hours , your body clock will reset , with whatever time you break your fast as morning .

# text = Tsechen Kunchab Ling : Temple of All - Encompassing Great Compassion .
# text = This is the seat of His Holiness the Sakya Trizin in the United States , a Tibetan Buddhist monastery established nine years ago .
# text = I spent the past weekend there .
# text = The field work office at my college arranges this retreat every semester .
# text = Everyone I 've talked to who has previously attended says wonderful things about it ; this semester , one of my friends told me she was going : I should join her !
# text = I like learning new things , so I signed up .

# text = A good decision : I did n't return all chill and zen , as one friend told me his roommate had , but I certainly gained a few new ideas and approaches to mull over , and dipped my hand into a previously unfamiliar piece of the world .

# text = The first evening , the twenty - something students -- most from my college , four from another -- gathered in the shrine room , sitting cross - legged on cushions as we listened to Khenpo Kalsang introduce Tibetan Buddhist philosophy .
# text = He began by telling us , " Do not take any of what I say on faith .
# text = Take it through analysis , if there is some benefit in it for you . "
# text = Religion , he said , is like a drugstore full of medicine .
# text = You do not go to the drugstore and buy everything in it -- you just buy what would be beneficial to you now .
# text = You believe the other medicine may have just as much value , but in other situations , not this one .
# text = We discussed the foundations : the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma ; the four noble truths ; karma ; defilements ; the six perfections .
# text = So , " a fellow student asked , " Giving one 's life for another being is the ultimate gift ? "
# text = Khenpo Kalsang , he smiled , and shook his head .
# text = " Only if you feel no regret , " he said .
# text = " If you feel regret , it destroys the merit . "
# text = Until then , preserve your own life , and do not give away anything that would cause you regret .
# text = Self - preservation above all else , unless the right situation arises .
# text = Later , I talked to the resident nun , Ani Kunga , about psychology and cognitive science .

# text = She had studied psychology for a while in grad school , but now holds the view that psychologists are going about understanding the mind and understanding the knower and what knowing is the wrong way . "
# text = Psychologists , " she said , " study the brain and the self externally .
# text = Ever since the 1920s , their science has been about observation of behavior , questionnaires , recordings of electrical brain activity .
# text = But the mind can only be known by you , the person whose mind it is . "
# text = She said philosophy and epistemology were doing it right : looking at experiences from the inside .
# text = A big overlap exists between Tibetan Buddhism , psychology and cognitive science .
# text = All three examine the distinction between the self and others , between the observer and the observed , between knowing and the knower .
# text = I agree with Ani Kunga to some extent -- only so much can be known about the mind from external observation .
# text = But this does n't mean that there is n't merit to such studies , nor that nothing of use can be learned in that way .
# text = Tibetan Buddhist philosophy also approaches the mind and the self from the inside .
# text = During a second philsophy session , Khenpo Kalsang translated a sutra about a king who received advice from the Buddha .
# text = This sutra delved into some questions about the nature of the self , whether the self is a delusion , and how the clinging of self is a defilement .
# text = I intend to discuss it in more depth later , so stay tuned .
# text = Compassion training and prayer flags
# text = In the afternoon , a group of us gathered outside for a meditation session with Ani Kunga .
# text = Sunshine melted lazily through the tree branches above , a breeze animating the branches ' shadows so they danced between our cushions .
# text = Compassion and anger were the session 's topics .
# text = The key message : " If there 's something you can do , why are you unhappy ?
# text = If there 's nothing you can do , why are you unhappy ? "
# text = All the methods built off the idea that you are in control : anger is an emotion , and you can change your emotions .
# text = Stay tuned for a more in - depth post on the topic .
# text = Another of the day 's activities was making prayer flags .
# text = As Ani Kunga explained , " Prayers , wishes , hopes , aspirations -- someone , many people , may share those with you .
# text = Hanging the prayer flag shares your prayer with everyone else in the world .
# text = This may do no good at all , but it may -- if everyone hopes and wishes and dreams and aspires , perhaps it will do good .
# text = But if no one shares their prayers , it will certainly do no good .
# text = So on the offchance that it will help , why not ? "
# text = This weekend reminded me that I 'm not done learning .

# text = If I stay still long enough , if I 've achieved a relatively constant level of happiness and satisfaction , I forget that I can and should continue to seek out new ideas and approaches , and incorporate beneficial ones into my life .
# text = A person is never " done , " and so , I 'll continue to observe and discuss and study , trying to pick the directions in which I 'll change , and trying to make tomorrow better than today .
# text = Ever onward and ever upward .
# text = Self - control , Self - efficacy , and New Year 's Resolutions Unresolved
# text = I 'm not one to make New Year 's resolutions .

# text = I mean , sure , I could take my pick of popular New Year 's resolutions ; I could decide , on the first day of the new year , that this year , I 'll start exercising more and eating better , or that I 'll spend more time with my family and friends , or that I 'll learn a new skill .
# text = Making resolutions : It 's about self - control

# text = The question Anirban Mukhopadhyay of the Hong Kong University and Gita Venkatarmani Johar of the Graduate School of Business at Columbia University asked is this : What determines how many goals a person will set , and how successful a person will be at achieving those goals ?
# text = They performed a few studies in 2005 to look at the relationship between self - control , goal setting , and goal achievement .
# text = In the paper , " self - control " is used to mean a sense of willpower .
# text = An important premise to note here is the idea that the probability of choosing a goal or making a resolution increases if a person thinks that goal can be attained .
# text = So if you think you 'll be able to achieve a goal , you 're more likely to set it .
# text = Combine this with theories of self - control , and in general , if you believe you have unlimited stores of self - control , you 'll set a larger number of goals .
# text = If you believe self - control is malleable but limited , you 'll set fewer goals .
# text = Mukhopadhyay & Venkatarmani also discuss self - efficacy : belief in one 's capabilities , the perceived ability to carry out a desired action .

# text = They propose that people with high self - efficacy -- people who believe that failure is the result of insufficient effort , and thus exhibit increased commitment and persistence -- will achieve more of their goals than people with low self - efficacy , who tend to view failure as the result of deficient ability , and thus may simply give up .
# text = Each passage contained two paragraphs ; the first discussed self - control either as limited or as unlimited , and the second discussed self - control as either malleable or fixed .

# text = The participants then answered questions about their belief in each of two theories presented , followed by a second questionnaire to assess motivation , in which they listed all their current goals .
# text = The study was testing whether a belief in unlimited , malleable self - control would result in most resolutions , and indeed , this is what was found .
# text = When lay theories were assessed first , this result reversed .
# text = The people who believed that self - control is fixed were unaffected by order .
# text = The third study moved on to examine goal achievement , adding a measure to look at self - efficacy .
# text = The study had two sessions , in November then February .
# text = Only 86 participants successfully returned for the second session , during which they indicated how much success they had had at keeping their resolutions .
# text = What does this mean for your resolutions ?

# text = As shown in the first two studies , more goals were set by people who believe self - control is unlimited and malleable than by any other people -- that is , if you expect more success , you may increase the difficulty and number of tasks that you set for yourself .
# text = Self - efficacy did not have a significant effect on goal - setting .
# text = As far as success goes , only the interaction between lay theory and self - efficacy was significant .
# text = If participants believed in limited self - control and were low in self - efficacy , they tended to give up more often , failing to achieve their goals .

# text = But if participants believed in unlimited self - control , self - efficacy had no effect ; participants achieved just as many goals regardless , and people who set more resolutions were marginally more likely to succeed .

# text = Mukhopadhyay & Venkatarmani realize that their research does not directly look at the relationship between lay theories of self - control and beliefs about one 's own amount of self - control and self - efficacy , and propose this as an area for future study .
# text = Varsity athletics : Credit or no ?
# text = It 's a matter of balance
# text = Vassar 's varsity athletes may soon receive academic credit for participating in their sports during the school year .
# text = This proposal has been in the works for nearly two years , and at long last , folks are voting to approve it .
# text = Or to not approve it , but the former seems more likely .
# text = As a member of the Student Athlete Advisory Committee and as a long - time varsity athlete , you might say I have particular stake in the proposal .

# text = After all , I could get half a unit a semester for up to four semesters -- a typical class is worth one unit , and a typical physical education course of any level is worth half a unit , with a maximum of two physical education units counting toward graduation requirements .

# text = It seems justified : Students can receive credit for participating in other extracurricular , faculty - supervised activities , such as the orchestra , the choir , and the repertory dance theatre , so why not varsity athletics ?
# text = My friend over at Carolyn Blogs agrees : from the above standpoint , sure , it seems fair to give credit to students .
# text = If you get credit for introductory P.E. classes , you should get credit for varsity athletics .

# text = But our school newspaper presents other arguments in favor , which Carolyn thinks are highly unjustified : On top of everything , we must remember that varsity athletics present a considerable time commitment .
# text = It is rare to find another activity on campus ? academic or extracurricular ? that includes a comparable daily rigor and frequent overnight obligation .
# text = Varsity athletes regularly travel throughout the northeastern to participate in meets , games and tournaments , often gone from campus for an entire weekend at a time .

# text = Although it 's certainly frustrating to travel to Boston for an all - day competition on the same weekend as a good friend 's birthday party , a fascinating - sounding lecture , a dance party , and seventeen other campus events no one in their right mind would ever want to miss , I agree with Carolyn .
# text = The reason I participate in my sport is because I enjoy it .
# text = If I cared more about other activities , I 'd do those instead .
# text = Simply being a huge time commitment is not a valid reason for awarding credit .

# text = Carolyn 's supporting example , that higher level courses with more difficult and plentiful homework are worth the same amount of credit as introductory 100 - level courses , drives this point home .

# text = And she 's backed up by our school 's system of awarding units instead of credit hours : This system ? which in its most basic form allots one unit of credit per semester course , regardless of difficulty , hours in class and subject matter ? makes Vassar relatively unique in its credit system .

# text = According to Registrar Dan Giannini , " The rationale behind such a system is to try to send the message that all courses are equal in worth and that one should n?t try to distinguish between courses based on time spent in or out of class . "

# text = The reason time commitment is highlighted is because , according to the authors of the article , the faculty " must consider what it can do to mitigate possible academic pressures on these students . "
# text = No , I do n't think the faculty has any obligation whatsoever .
# text = Students choose to be varsity athletes of their own accord .
# text = If they ca n't manage to balance their athletics and their coursework , then perhaps they should reconsider participating in a varsity sport in the first place .
# text = Athletes should n't get special privileges simply because they 're athletes .
# text = Sacrifices must be made , sure : Dance party on Friday night , or overnight travel to a competition ?
# text = The question is , what 's more important to me ?

# text = The article continues : While athletes will continue to be held to the College RSQUOs rigorous academic standards , the athletics credit could discourage a varsity athlete from unnecessarily taking on five academic credits while in their athletic season .

# text = With the proposed varsity credit , the athlete seeking to assume five courses in his or her athletic season will be checked with an overload form , thus encouraging the student to think twice about assuming such a large academic and extracurricular load .

# text = I 'd like to be known that students who have trouble balancing tough course loads and time - consuming extracurriculars have always had the option of taking a lighter load or dropping an extracurricular .
# text = Adding the option of a varsity unit to the list does n't make much of a difference .
# text = Students who are n't varsity athletes could add an easy P.E. course instead .
# text = Students who can balance their work and their sport will continue to do so .
# text = And let it be known , varsity athletes do n't have to take a half unit for their sport ... thus negating the need for an overload form if taking five courses .
# text = Carolyn says , in response to the above quote , that " participating in sports is optional , and should always take second place to academics . "
# text = Academics are officially what college is about .
# text = Academics are what get graded .
# text = Students ' GPAs will , in part , determine what they are able to do with their lives .
# text = But academics are only one particular kind of knowledge .
# text = Carolyn 's statement assumes that a student can learn more important things from academics than from participation on a sports team .

# text = Personally , though , some of the most important things I 've learned about persistence , goal - setting , success and excellence , effort , teamwork , leadership .... these I 've learned from my sport and my coaches .
# text = It 's a different kind of knowledge than what one typically gains in an academic course , yes .
# text = But it 's no less important .
# text = And that , I think , is the best reason for awarding credit for varsity athletics .
# text = Detroit and the Myth of the $ 100 House |
# text = Uprooted , an eco $$ travel blog
# text = America 's Rust Belt is a swath of cities and towns that boomed during the Industrial Era and now lie -- well , rusting -- as empty remainders of glory days past .
# text = Chief among these is Detroit , Motor City .
# text = The longtime center of American automotive manufacturing was gutted when the Big Three car companies simultaneously failed .
# text = Detroit , already plagued by corruption and crime , saw its unemployment rate skyrocket in 2009 .
# text = What 's left behind when an economy collapses ?
# text = Cheap real estate , that 's what .
# text = I 'd read a New York Times article about some forward - thinking artist - types who bought a house in Detroit for $ 1,900 .
# text = In fact , the article went on , soon a nearby house went on the market for $ 100 .
# text = The artist types notified their buddies , who moved in post haste .
# text = Even if it was a real fixer - upper , even if you really were better off tearing it down than living in it , that 'd still be a hell of a deal .
# text = Why , out in New Mexico , where you can still buy unincorporated land with no water or roads , you 'd pay at least $ 1,000 for a house - sized plot of dust .
# text = So how can you buy an actual home for $ 100 ?
# text = That 's literally cheaper than dirt .
# text = The possibilities of this were fascinating .
# text = I had visions of hipsters from coast to coast converging in Detroit , building a new city on rock & roll .
# text = I pictured young artists owning homes , fixing up neighborhoods .
# text = I saw community gardens , art parks , a grassroots transformation of a city .
# text = We could take that oil - stained soil and those rusted factories , and create something new and beautiful .
# text = With houses going for $ 100 , I thought , what would you have to lose by moving to Detroit ?
# text = And so Quiet Earp and I did some research , and came up with a list of houses selling for under a grand .
# text = We had plenty to choose from : there were more cheap houses than we would have time to visit .
# text = We picked two neighborhoods to cruise , and dove in .
# text = But once we entered Detroit , the truth hit fast : this is a modern American ghost town .
# text = The place is practically deserted .
# text = Its streets , built wide to accommodate heavy traffic , are mostly empty .
# text = Houses and businesses are boarded up , painted up , bombed out and falling down .
# text = Even in the center of the business district , there 's no traffic and hardly any people .
# text = I videotaped it : It got worse as we drove into residential areas , looking for those cheap houses .
# text = In fact , I 've never felt so out of place in all my life .
# text = Even in Chicago 's South Side , where we counted five white people in an hour , I felt fine just driving around ; not so in Detroit .
# text = Truthfully , it was n't about race : it was about being naive .
# text = It was about driving down streets where we truly did not belong and were not welcome .
# text = Detroit is a ghost town , and it 's inhabited by ghosts : the only people left here are those who ca n't or wo n't leave .
# text = They live in deserted neighborhoods , in houses with collapsed front steps and missing windows .
# text = They sit on the porch and watch the cars go by , watch the deals go down , watch their neighborhoods crumble .
# text = And we , driving through slowly and reading house numbers in a late - model Honda , stuck out like a couple of thumbs .
# text = So we sped up , and went straight to the houses .
# text = Sometimes we stopped to take a photo , but mostly we did n't .
# text = Earp and I have each lived happily in the wilds of West Oakland , but the danger I felt in Detroit was like nothing I 'd experienced before .
# text = I was actually afraid for my life .
# text = The New York Times correspondent wrote that his friend Mitch 's $ 1,900 home " had already been stripped of its appliances and wiring ...
# text = But for Mitch that only added to its appeal , because he now had the opportunity to renovate it with solar heating , solar electricity and low - cost , high - efficiency appliances . "
# text = It " needed some work , a hole patched , some windows replaced . "
# text = Well , I do n't know what part of Detroit these folks live in , but the $ 100 houses I saw looked more like this : You see , abandoned houses in this town get set on fire .
# text = Wherever we went in those neighborhoods , one in four houses had been torched .
# text = On one corner , we saw a giant banner hung across a charred front porch .
# text = We did n't slow down to take a photo , but I 'll paraphrase : DO N'T BURN HOUSES DOWN !
# text = DETROIT POLICE ARE WATCHING YOU !
# text = Except that they obviously are n't .
# text = People who live in this part of town are on their own .
# text = And although I and many others would love to own even a fire - scarred , condemned building , the fact is that we would n't last a week here .

# text = Buy a $ 100 house in Detroit , and you get a lifetime supply of sleepless nights : you 'll spend the next several years waiting for burglars and arsonists , murderers and crackheads to break in the windows .
# text = It 's like the Wild West without the scenery , the gold , and the hope .
# text = Ultimately , I do believe that change will come to Detroit .

# text = A man in his early 20s recently asked me , " So what 's a recession like ? "

# text = That lesson is the " Stockdale Paradox , " a peculiar psychology shown by those who emerge from tough times not just intact , but stronger .
# text = Adm. Jim Stockdale was the highest - ranking U.S. military officer in the Hanoi prison camp during the Vietnam War .

# text = Tortured many times during his 8 - year imprisonment , Stockdale lived without any prisoner 's rights , no set release date and no certainty as to whether he would ever again see his family .
# text = He shouldered the burden of command while fighting an internal war against his captors and their attempts to use the prisoners for propaganda .

# text = At one point , he beat himself with a stool and cut himself with a razor , deliberately disfiguring himself so that he could not be put on video as an example of a " well - treated prisoner . "
# text = He exchanged secret intelligence information with his wife through their letters knowing that discovery would mean more torture and perhaps death .
# text = After his release , Stockdale became the first three - star officer in the history of the Navy to wear both aviator wings and the Congressional Medal of Honor .

# text = My conversation with Stockdale had a profound influence on me , but I never really considered it a business lesson until my research team began to wrestle with the question of why some companies rise from difficulty to become great while others emerge from those exact same difficulties weakened and dispirited .
# text = We found that companies that became great embraced a corporate version of the Stockdale Paradox .
# text = Fannie Mae , for example found itself in the 1982 recession losing $ 1M every business day , with $ 56B in loans under water .
# text = Many analysts thought Fannie Mae , which was getting 9 % on its mortgage portfolio but paying 15 % on the debt it issued , was doomed .
# text = But CEO David Maxwell and his team never wavered in their aim to not merely survive , but also to prevail as a great company .

# text = But they used this grim fact as a catalyst for creating an entirely new business model based on asking three central questions of greatness : What can we potentially do better than any other company in the world ? What can best drive our economic engine ? What best ignites the passions of our people ?
# text = Instead of reacting to the recession with mindless restructuring , Fannie Mae rebuilt itself based on its answers to these questions .
# text = Eventually , it generated investor returns nearly eight times those of the general stock market .
# text = When asked how he dealt with the nay Sayers and the analysts who wrote Fannie Mae off , Maxwell said that it was never an issue inside the company .
# text = " Of course , we had to stop doing a lot of stupid things , but we never entertained the possibility that we would fail .
# text = We were going to use the calamity as an opportunity to remake Fannie Maw into a great company . "
# text = The sad truth is that most executive teams wo n't respond that way to these dark days of uncertainty .

# text = Instead of using this recession as an opportunity to fundamentally rethink their business and rebuild a culture of discipline , the will simply restructure , lay off a bunch of people and liquidate their cultural equity .
# text = Mediocre leaders will hold out false hopes for a quick fix , only to watch those hopes be swept away by events .
# text = Their companies will begin to die of a broken heart .
# text = It need not be this way .

# text = Those who lead with the Stockdale Paradox - those who retain the unwavering faith that they will find a way to prevail in the end , but who also retain the discipline to confront the most brutal facts of reality - will find this an ideal time to rebuild and reinforce greatness .
# text = Used correctly , this recession can be a defining time in your firm 's history that , in retrospect , you would not trade .
# text = Used wrongly , this recession will weaken your foundations and make it that much harder to become great .

# text = 3. Credit Concerns Regarding Authority Granted to DWR in AB1X to Purchase Electricity on Behalf of the Utilities
# text = Enron responded to the RFP issued by DWR to enter into power contracts with suppliers .
# text = However , ambiguities contained in AB1X have created significant credit risk concerns that need to be resolved in order to finalize contract terms .

# text = Enron has proposed several options for resolving the credit risk issues and is working with DWR to arrive at a solution that is mutually agreeable to both sides and that might serve as a template for power purchase agreements going forward .
# text = Summary of the Source of the Credit Risk Issue
# text = The language in AB1X is ambiguous as to whether DWR has any authority to charge California ratepayers for the costs of purchasing power .
# text = From our analysis of the bill , the language in AB1X appears to leave intact the California PUC ,s exclusive jurisdiction over ratemaking in California .
# text = Ambiguous Regulatory Authority Regarding Contract " Prudence "
# text = The language in AB1X leaves open the possibility that the California Public Utilities Commission could determine that power purchases made by DWR are " imprudent . "
# text = Ambiguous Language Regarding the Ratemaking Mechanism that Will Be Used to Recover DWR ,s Costs of Power Purchases

# text = Moreover , as currently drafted , it is difficult to determine whether AB1X would even permit the PUC to include in rates all of the charges necessary to fully recover DWR ,s power purchase costs .
# text = Again , this ambiguity raises significant credit risk concerns since suppliers have little assurance that DWR will have the ability to recover from ratepayers the costs of purchasing power .
# text = Options to Resolve Concerns Regarding Credit Risk
# text = We have identified three options :
# text = This is the preferred option , though we understand that the there may be some political challenges standing in the way of amending AB1X .
# text = Clarify the Ambiguities in AB1X through an Order Issued by the PUC , and through Contract Language

# text = We have attached electronic copies of the talking points related to the order that the California PUC would need to issue under this option .
# text = Make Use of Other Instruments Designed to Address Credit Risk

# text = DWR officials have indicated to us that DWR prefers to pursue the second options .
# text = That is , DWR prefers to clarify the ambiguities in AB1X through a PUC order and through contract amendments .

# text = This is an open letter to David Hardy , author of Bowling for Columbine : Documentary or Fiction ? , probably the most comprehensive among many rebuttals of the Oscar - winning documentary .
# text = Critics have now gone so far as to call for the revocation of the award .
# text = Their chances are small , however , as their arguments rely on polemic , exaggeration and misrepresentation -- in other words , on the same techniques which they accuse Moore of using .
# text = Dear David Hardy , It is fascinating to watch the organized character assassination of Michael Moore that has been going on in the United States since the release of his last documentary .

# text = In a time of simple - minded patriotism , loud , clear and dissenting voices like Mr. Moore 's are perceived as disturbing and have to be silenced , partially through well funded public relations campaigns , partially through conservative " grass - roots " propaganda .
# text = Not surprisingly , much of the criticism of Moore 's film is misguided or outright wrong , often vastly more inaccurate than Moore 's work itself .

# text = Moore portrays the NRA as an unethical , dishonest organization ; he sees the paranoia and fear in the United States as a primary cause of violence , and he does not see gun ownership itself as a problem .
# text = His documentary is full of subtle humor , jaw - dropping dialogue and dark contrasts .
# text = All in all , it is an accurate portrayal of America 's gun and violence culture .
# text = It also raises questions about America 's foreign policy of recent decades , questions which have been all but ignored by Moore 's critics .
# text = On your webpage , you state that " Moore 's resolution is questionable .

# text = After all , early in the movie he discards the possibility that playing violent video games and watching violent flicks can cause violence -- because Canadians like , and Japanese positively love , those .
# text = If violent movies and violent videogames can not cause violence -- then how can newscasts about violence do so ? "
# text = This is a faulty generalization .

# text = There is a huge difference , for example , between playing a game like " Quake " and listening to a radio broadcast that tells you that your family will be killed unless you take action to kill others now .
# text = The latter is the kind of media propaganda that was used to unleash a genocide in Rwanda in 1994 , which killed 800,000 people .
# text = Obviously , media propaganda can incite people to kill .

# text = Interactive fiction like video games , on the other hand , presents violence in a narrative context , which may very well desensitize participants to said violence , but no causative link has ever been proven .
# text = This is consistent with the kind of media - incited violence described above , and in no relationship whatsoever to the theory of video game or music incited violence .

# text = Moore 's second hypothesis is that America 's foreign policy may contribute to the belief that violence is an appropriate means to solve conflicts , a hypothesis which is shared by many sociologists and psychologists .
# text = Children who grow up in war - torn regions are known for having similar views -- war is perceived as a normal part of existence , violence as a natural way to solve disputes .

# text = In a weaker sense , the same message is projected to American children , who grow up being told that it is not acceptable to be violent to one another , but who simultaneously have to endure corporal punishment and media messages about how " the enemies of freedom " are punished .
# text = Moore 's film was made before the dead bodies of Qusay and Uday Hussein were paraded on national TV .
# text = Americans were gloating over this demented corpse show : " They squealed like little piggies too , so you 'll have to make do with ' oink , oink , squeeeeeeeallll ' for their last words .
# text = That goes for your grandson Mustafa too , by the way .
# text = Still think fucking with the U.S. was a good idea , Sammy ? "
# text = Mustafa was 14 years when he was killed .
# text = Americans cheer the killing of children , yet wonder why their own children grow up to be more violent than those in other nations .
# text = It is paradoxical notions like this one which Moore 's film seeks to address .
# text = Your webpage list a number of alleged inaccuracies in Moore 's movies .
# text = It is true that Moore 's film is sometimes unintentionally deceptive , but to call it fraudulent is hyperbole to the extreme .
# text = It is no more so than any other successful documentary of the last decades .
# text = Let 's look at some specific criticisms :
# text = Critics have stated that this scene was " staged " , but in the bank interview , the official tells Moore that the bank has its own vault storing about 500 weapons at any given time .

# text = This sounds more like a later correction for public relations purposes , but of course nobody questions the bank claims when they can be used against Moore .

# text = There is nothing inaccurate whatsoever about the bank scene .

# text = Infiltrating insect societies , however , is much simpler .

# text = The red harvester ant lives in hot , dry deserts , building its nests in light yellowy sand and foraging for seeds deposited by winds and rain .
# text = Because of this , I will ignore other ant species in the design of Antie , and will not create a fighting behavior .

# text = Queens and drones will not be considered in this proposal , as their behaviors and design is much more specialized and would be applicable only during the breeding season , which occurs but once per year .
# text = The behaviors of the sterile workers may be divided into several subcategories : brood care , nest maintenance , patrolling and foraging .
# text = Little is known about brood care , as this occurs only in the deepest regions of the nest and observation would generally require the destruction of the nest .

# text = It is therefore these three behaviors that I would like to focus on in this proposal : the others remain a bit too mysterious to yet model , and the ability of a robot to pass undetected in the depths of a colony would be very difficult to observe .

# text = Before beginning an analysis of any piece by Béla Bartók , one must first decide to what degree tonal analysis will be used .
# text = Bartók RSQUOs music , although it is often difficult to call completely tonal , never entirely sheds itself of tonal elements and structure .
# text = This remains true even with one of his last compositions , the Concerto for Orchestra , written two years before his death in 1943 .
# text = The discussion that follows analyzes the first movement of the Concerto , focusing on the tonal structures at play throughout the movement .
# text = The analysis will treat the movement tonally , investigating the progression of local " tonics " and its relationship to the overall form .

# text = We will also examine to what degree a " tonal " reading of this movement is limited in its analytical potential in an attempt to pinpoint exactly where Bartók strays from common - practice compositional techniques .
# text = Bartók describes the form of the first movement as " more or less regular sonata form . " Bartók , 431 .
# text = The " backwards " recapitulation is a technique that Bartók employs frequently because of the formal symmetry it creates .

# text = The middle pitch of the descent , B , acts as the " dominant " to F , based on its symmetrical division of the whole - tone scale and the fact that the second theme appears in B in the exposition .
# text = Bartók has often applied a tonic - dominant relationship to a pitch - class and its tritone partner , and even admits to using that as a compositional framework in his fifth string quartet .

# text = In this particular movement , Bartók feigns moving to the tonal dominant , C , for the second theme before reinterpreting C as a chromatic passing tone between D♭ and B ? this and other subtleties shown in Example 2 will be explained in detail in later sections .

# text = As Paul Wilson points out , the title " Introduzione " given to the movement as a whole seems to apply only to the first 75 measures .

# text = The Introduction does not relate thematically to any of the main sections of the movement ? in fact , it is the third movement that draws its thematic material from this section ? but the harmonic and motivic principles at play here foreshadow some important elements of the entire piece .
# text = To begin with , the opening motive in the celli and basses , shown in Example 3 , outlines a pentatonic set and strongly presents C♯ as the tonal center .
# text = The pentatonic set here is exclusively a pitch - class set , and its incarnations throughout the movement are devoid of any connotations associated with the pentatonic scale .
# text = Indeed , this set can be seen more as a by-product of stacked perfect fourths than a generative element itself .

# text = The perfect fourth in fact generates much of the motivic and harmonic material of the entire movement , and its importance is immediately evident in the Introduction with the opening bass motive .

# text = Furthermore , the following two instances of this opening motive , shown in Examples 4 and 5 , remove any doubt as to the motivic importance of the perfect fourth , and in turn diminish the importance of the pentatonic set .
# text = Example 4 transitions from C♯ to F♯ , and adds pitch - class E to the pentatonic set of Example 3 , creating a six - note set of stacked fourths .
# text = Example 5 shows the true dominance of the perfect fourth ; the set created is a ten - note set derived by stacking fourths .
# text = If we begin from the final D♯ and ascend the circle of fourths until we reach C we obtain the entire set presented in this example .
# text = The overall motion in the first 29 measures is C♯ to D♯ , through F♯ ; these are represented enharmonically in Example 2 as D♭ , E♭ and G♭ .
# text = As previously mentioned , this motion constitutes the initial ascent to what will eventually be a whole - tone descent from F to F .

# text = We can connect the two by noting that the descending whole step consists of two ascending fourths ; indeed , the structural whole - tone descent is often " filled in " with the intervening fourth .
# text = This sequence of intervals is the inversion of those found in the second head motive of the first theme of the exposition , shown in measures 2 - 3 of Example 8 .

# text = So although there is no thematic relation between the Introduction and the main sections of the movement , within the first 29 measures we can already see structural , harmonic and motivic elements that apply to the movement as a whole .

# text = While both stories each characterize Madame White Snake fairly consistently within their narratives , the uneven characterization in film noir perhaps mirrors the evolution of her character over time : readers may not be sure whether she is a pure villainess or whether she is a good wife who is badly treated by society , because there is evidence of both throughout her legend .
