# text = U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell arrived here on Tuesday night for meetings with fellow foreign ministers aimed at solidifying a second front , in Southeast Asia , in the campaign against global terrorism .
# text = But he has had to balance that goal with longstanding concerns about human rights abuses in the region .

# text = In meetings on Tuesday in Malaysia and Singapore before touching down in this oil - producing sultanate for two days of talks with members of the Association of South East Asian Nations , Powell said he repeatedly raised the issue .
# text = " We still believe strongly in human rights , and that everything we do has to be consistent with universal standards of human rights , " he said .

# text = But at a news conference in Singapore , Powell hinted that the Bush administration was ready to discuss resuming military cooperation with Indonesia , the world 's most populous Muslim nation and a sometimes reluctant partner in the efforts to crack down on militant Islamic groups .
# text = The United States cut virtually all military links with Indonesia in 1999 after its forces were implicated in the violence that swept East Timor after that territory voted for independence .

# text = On Thursday , Powell and representatives of the nations of the Asian group , including Indonesia , are expected to sign a declaration promising cooperation to prevent terrorism by sharing information , blocking funds , tightening borders and making it hard to use forged travel papers .

# text = " We recognized that terrorism is a global threat and that the disturbing acts of terrorism and transnational crimes , which continue to threaten world peace and stability , must be tackled by the international community , " the ministers said in a communique on Tuesday .
# text = Powell is among the representatives from 13 nations outside Southeast Asia , including China , Japan and Russia , that are taking part in the annual meeting of the group 's regional forum .
# text = Terrorism dominates the agenda , though the possibility of a meeting here between Powell and his North Korean counterpart , Paek Nam Sun , has generated the most news .
# text = It would be the highest - level contact between the United States and North Korea since President Bush took office .
# text = Powell heads to Indonesia 's capital , Jakarta , late on Thursday before finishing a weeklong trip through the region in the Philippines on Saturday .
# text = He said that when he arrives in Jakarta , he will have " some ideas and some initiatives " to present to President Megawati Sukarnoputri .

# text = Indonesia is already receiving $ 400,000 in the current fiscal year for civilian training programs and is to receive a like amount next year ; and the United States expects to provide an additional $ 16 million this year to train police officers in counterterrorism .
# text = At the same time , the Pentagon is reviewing how to allocate another $ 17 million in " counterterrorism fellowships , " some of which could go to Indonesia .

# text = But a senior State Department official also acknowledged that some in the administration and Congress are pushing for more direct military cooperation , which would require congressional approval .

# text = " I think they recognize the danger that we all face and I think they have been cooperating more fully with us as time goes by , and I 'm quite sure that Mrs. Megawati is committed to this cause , " Powell said in Singapore .
# text = He met there with Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong , who endorsed the idea of renewed military ties between the United States and Indonesia as an important step in stabilizing that country .
# text = Powell contended that it was not inconsistent to want to foster cooperation even with an organization like the Indonesian military , which has a history of human rights abuses .
# text = " If you get young officers , expose them to a military organization that is within a democratic political institution , such as the United States , then that rubs off on them , " he said .
# text = In Malaysia , Powell met with Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad , who has led the country since 1981 .

# text = The Malaysian foreign minister , Syed Hamid Albar , later told local reporters that Powell had proposed that American and Malaysian officials review the idea of forming a regional training center in Malaysia to coordinate antiterrorism activities .

# text = His brief stop in Malaysia also highlighted the moral ambiguities of the effort to prevent terrorism and its emphasis on cooperation with governments that the United States has often criticized .

# text = The United States once distanced itself from Mahathir for strong - arm tactics with political rivals , and human rights groups criticize him for arresting and jailing scores of suspected militants , including some who may be linked to al-Qaida , without trial .

# text = With the barrage of crack cocaine - connected killings in the 1980s came the realization that young people were too often full - fledged players in the violence .

# text = So , Starke matched a problem with a problem and found a solution .

# text = RARE COIN FETCHES RECORD $ 7.59 MILLION AT AUCTION

# text = The 1933 double eagle , a $ 20 gold piece with a mysterious history that involves a president , a king and a Secret Service sting operation , was auctioned Tuesday last night for a record price for a coin , $ 7.59 million , nearly double the previous record .
# text = The anonymous buyer , believed to be an individual collector who lives in the United States , made the winning bid in a fiercely contested nine - minute auction at Sotheby 's in Manhattan .

# text = Eight bidders were joined by 500 coin collectors and dealers in an auction house audience seemingly devoid of celebrity bidders , while an additional 534 observers followed the bidding on eBay .

# text = As auction houses prepare for their fall seasons in an uncertain economy , the sale price " suggests that the marketplace for important items is enormously strong , " said David Redden , a vice chairman at Sotheby 's , who was the auctioneer .
# text = " This is an astonishing new record for a coin , " he said .

# text = In an unprecedented move , the auction proceeds were split by the U.S. Mint and a London coin dealer , Stephen Fenton , who had won that right in court after having been arrested by Secret Service agents for trying to sell the coin in the Waldorf - Astoria Hotel in Manhattan in 1996 .

# text = Henrietta Holsman Fore , the director of the U.S. Mint , who witnessed the sale , said , " The monies we receive will go toward helping to pay down the debt and to fight the war on terrorism . "
# text = Fenton commented that the double eagle had been on " a long historic journey , with a very satisfying ending . "
# text = He added , " I am thrilled with the price . "
# text = The previous numismatic record holder was an 1804 U.S. silver dollar , which sold for $ 4.14 million in 1999 .
# text = Sotheby 's partner in the one - lot auction was Stack 's Rare Coins , with which it shared the customary 15 percent commission .
# text = " I have never seen as much interest in the sale of any coin in my 30 years in the business , " said Lawrence R. Stack , the company 's managing director .
# text = " This is the Mona Lisa of coins , " said Beth Deisher , editor of Coin World , the largest weekly coin publication in the United States , with a circulation of 85,000 .
# text = Collectors ' Web sites have surged with speculation about the sale price , and enthusiasts even organized betting pools .
# text = On Tuesday night , Redden took the podium for nine minutes before the gavel came down , recognizing bidders in the audience and on the telephone .
# text = The tension in the crowd was broken with a burst of applause after the $ 5 million mark , and a louder explosion at $6 million .
# text = The rumor in the crowd had been that " anything under $ 6 million would be a bargain , " said Ute Wartenberg , executive director of the American Numismatic Society in Manhattan .
# text = Most bidders dropped out after that price .
# text = The gavel sounded at $6.6 million after a Sotheby 's senior vice president , Selby Kiffer , made the final bid for the anonymous buyer on the telephone .
# text = The sale price of $ 6.6 million , when added to the commission , totaled $ 7.59 million .

# text = The auction attendance was swelled by coin collectors who had gathered on the eve of the American Numismatic Association Convention , the largest coin show of the year , expected to draw more than 10,000 people to the Marriott Marquis Hotel Wednesday .
# text = " So the auction was almost like the ribbon - cutting ceremony for the convention , " Stack said .
# text = Fore of the mint said the high price for the coin was reached " because it is one of a kind , it is beautiful and it has a great story . "

# text = The coin was the only 1933 double eagle that has ever been legally offered for sale , and its Maltese Falconesque history only recently came to light , thanks to documents unearthed during the five - year legal battle over its ownership .
# text = In 1792 , it was deemed that all gold and silver U.S. coins would bear the depiction of an eagle , but gold pieces were issued only after a gold rush boom in 1850 .
# text = They were called double eagles because their face value was twice that of the original $ 10 gold piece .

# text = Following the suggestion of President Theodore Roosevelt , the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens redesigned the coin in 1907 in high relief , forever after giving the coins the designation " saints . "

# text = But in 1933 , President Franklin D. Roosevelt took the United States off the gold standard , and ordered all the 1933 saints already manufactured destroyed , save for two reserved for the Smithsonian Institution .
# text = They were never declared legal currency .
# text = Presumably after being stolen by a mint employee , nine double eagles surfaced during the mid-1940s and 1950s .
# text = They were seized by the Secret Service and melted down .

# text = But before these coins came to light , the royal legation of Egypt turned up with one at the Department of the Treasury , and somehow got an official to issue an export license for the coin to enhance the collection of King Farouk .
# text = By the time that blunder was discovered , the coin had left the United States .
# text = In 1954 , after the king was deposed , his coins were sold at auction and the double eagle vanished .
# text = It went underground until it came to Fenton in 1995 .

# text = His arrest in Manhattan , after attempting to sell the coin for $ 1.5 million , led to a court battle over whether -- thanks to the Treasury 's mistaken export permission in 1944 -- the coin could be legally owned .
# text = The double eagle came close to being melted down many times .

# text = The coin once again escaped destruction when it was moved from the Treasury Department vault in 7 World Trade Center eight months before the building collapsed after the Sept. 11 terrorist attack .
# text = The record price was seen as a gift by coin collectors .
# text = " Many people believe that our great coin rarities are vastly undervalued in comparison to old master paintings , " Deisher said .
# text = In a ceremony after the sale , Fore of the mint declared the coin the only 1933 double eagle ever to be legally issued by the U.S. government .
# text = This " monetized " the coin , making it legal tender .
# text = The buyer will receive a certificate of transfer stating just that , but only after paying the auction price and a fee of $ 20 for the face value of the coin .

# text = NEW JERSEY SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS TRANSSEXUAL 'S DEATH SENTENCE
# text = The New Jersey Supreme Court on Tuesday overturned the death sentence of Leslie Ann Nelson , a transsexual go-go dancer who killed a police officer and an investigator with an AK-47 rifle .

# text = The court , vacating Nelson 's death sentence for the second time , ruled on two grounds : that the jury could have been confused by instructions on the verdict sheet and that the prosecutor made improper accusations in his closing argument .
# text = Nelson , 44 , had been the only woman of 14 people on New Jersey 's death row .
# text = The ruling , which does not affect Nelson 's guilty plea , sends the case back to the trial court for resentencing .
# text = The state attorney general 's office has not decided whether to seek the death penalty again , a spokesman , Peter Aseltine , said Tuesday .
# text = The court upheld the sentence of another death row inmate , Robert O. Marshall , convicted of arranging the murder of his wife at a picnic area on the Garden State Parkway .

# text = In its 5 - to - decision in the Nelson case , the court showed continuing uneasiness with the death penalty , as it has done even since adopting a voluminous set of review procedures in 1999 to govern capital cases .
# text = New Jersey has not had an execution since 1963 .

# text = Justice James R. Zazzali and Justice Virginia Long said in a separate opinion that in addition to the reasons given in the majority opinion , also written by Zazzali , they believed the death penalty would constitute cruel and unusual punishment because of Nelson 's history of emotional disturbance .

# text = Zazzali and Long had expressed similar reservations in June 2001 when the court overturned the death sentence of Thomas J. Koskovich , who was 18 when he killed two pizza deliverymen in an ambush .
# text = The majority opinion Tuesday said the court would impose higher standards in capital cases when reviewing prosecutors ' conduct and possibly ambiguous jury instructions .

# text = While all five members of the majority found the instructions to the jury on weighing aggravating and mitigating factors to be confusing , two of those justices wrote in a partial dissent that the prosecutor 's statements in his summation about the defense 's expert witnesses were within the bounds of acceptable argument .
# text = Two of the court 's members , Chief Justice Deborah T. Poritz and Justice Peter G. Verniero , did not participate in the Nelson case because both are former attorneys general .

# text = EDITORIAL : THE SHAME OF EGYPT
# text = The New York Times said in an editorial for Wednesday , July 31 : President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt describes himself as America 's leading Arab ally .
# text = Yet his anti-democratic behavior is an embarrassment to Washington and an affront to his own people .

# text = The latest example is Monday 's re-sentencing of Saad Eddin Ibrahim , a sociologist and human rights activist , to seven years in prison for his efforts to register voters , monitor elections and report attacks on Egypt 's Coptic Christians .
# text = Ibrahim , who holds dual United States and Egyptian citizenship , is 63 years old and ailing .
# text = The verdict should be annulled , not just on humanitarian grounds but because his prosecution is an abrogation of the most basic standards of justice .
# text = Ibrahim 's harsh punishment sends a chilling message to Egyptians yearning for a more accountable and tolerant society .
# text = Egyptian courts are neither fair nor independent .
# text = Like every other government institution , they hew closely to Mubarak 's wishes .
# text = That is especially true of the State Security Court that ruled in this case .
# text = Ibrahim might never have been tried had he not written an article taking note of Mubarak 's efforts to create a presidential dynasty .

# text = Nor is it likely his sentence would have been reaffirmed if Mubarak believed that convicting an American citizen for promoting democracy and human rights might jeopardize his own standing with the Bush administration and the $ 2 billion annual American subsidy that keeps his government afloat .
# text = That aid bonanza was granted to reward Mubarak 's predecessor , Anwar Sadat , for signing a peace treaty with Israel .
# text = Washington has never demanded good governance and democracy from Cairo in return .
# text = In recent months President Bush has spoken of the need to promote democracy in the Arab world .
# text = But so far he has pushed the point only with the Palestinians .
# text = It is time to extend this policy to Egypt .

# text = The New York Times said in an editorial for Wednesday , July 31 : Responding to a wave of public dismay over the first designs for rebuilding Lower Manhattan , Gov. George Pataki has sent word that it 's time to go back to the drawing board .

# text = EDITORIAL : A PALLID CLEAN AIR PLAN

# text = The New York Times said in an editorial for Wednesday , July 31 : President Bush has now unveiled his long - awaited " Clear Skies " proposal , which he promises will simplify and strengthen the Clean Air Act without crippling American industry .
# text = A debate on how to make the 32 - year - old Clean Air Act a stronger and more efficient instrument is surely long overdue .
# text = But the Bush plan falls well short of the only other credible proposal on the table , a bill sponsored by Sen. James Jeffords , Independent of Vermont .
# text = Like Jeffords , the president calls for substantial reductions in three major pollutants -- the nitrogen oxides that produce smog , sulfur dioxide , which causes acid rain , and mercury .
# text = But he ignores emissions of carbon dioxide , the main global warming gas .
# text = That is a huge omission .
# text = Even for the pollutants he addresses , Bush 's timetable is too leisurely .
# text = He aims to reduce all three by 70 percent by 2018 .
# text = The Jeffords proposal would make the same sizable reductions by 2008 .
# text = Finally , the Bush proposal would roll back key provisions of the existing Clean Air Act that Jeffords would keep .

# text = Bush argues that the regulatory mechanisms he has in mind for reaching Clear Skies ' goals , chiefly a market - based emissions trading scheme , will be so effective that the need for many existing rules will disappear .

# text = The Bush bill , as written , is not the way to get there .

# text = OLYMPIC JUDGING SCANDAL DEEPENS WITH ARREST OF RUSSIAN CRIME FIGURE
# text = New York Times News Service

# text = A Russian accused of being in organized crime was arrested in Italy on Wednesday on an American complaint that he conspired to fix the pairs figure skating and ice dancing competitions at the recent Salt Lake Winter Olympics , which were dominated by the sport 's judging scandals .

# text = The Russian , Alimzhan Tokhtakhounov , who was arrested by the Italian authorities at his resort home in Forte dei Marmi , appeared to have a singular motivation for rigging the competitions : getting a visa to return to France , where he once lived .

# text = The federal prosecutor in Manhattan alleged in a criminal complaint that Tokhtakhounov had conceived and directed a scheme with a second man alleged to be in the Russian mob and a member of the Russian Skating Federation to secure a gold medal for the top Russian pairs skaters and for the top French ice dancers , one of whom is a Russian .

# text = The Russian team of Yelena Berezhnaya and Anton Sikharulidze narrowly won the gold medal over the Canadians Jamie Sale and David Pelletier , who were later awarded a duplicate gold medal because of the ensuing judging controversy .
# text = Sale and Pelletier declined to comment on Wednesday .
# text = The French ice dancers , Marina Anissina and Gwendal Peizerat , later won the gold over a Russian team .
# text = The complaint casts the Salt Lake City figure skating scandal in a more serious light than the cronyism and vote - swapping that have tainted the increasingly troubled sport .

# text = Over the past four years , four judges have been suspended , including a Ukrainian who was taped by a Canadian judge detailing the order of finish for the ice dancers before the 1998 Winter Games in Nagano , Japan .

# text = If convicted of the charges against him -- conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit bribery , both felonies _ Tokhtakhounov faces maximum prison time of 10 years and a fine of $ 500,000 or more .
# text = The United States is seeking his extradition from Italy .
# text = The Italian authorities provided the FBI with information from wiretaps of Tokhtakhounov 's home telephone , part of an investigation into his criminal activities .

# text = The FBI said explicit conversations about the scheme had been recorded between Tokhtakhounov and his conspirators , and between him and Anissina , who was born in Russia and skated for France , and her mother .
# text = The FBI cited a vivid conversation with Anissina 's mother in which Tokhtakhounov assured her that even if her daughter " falls , we will make sure she is No. 1 . "

# text = After the Winter Olympics , a French judge , Marie-Reine Le Gougne , was suspended by the International Skating Union for not reporting pressure she said was put on her by Didier Gailhaguet , president of the French Skating Federation , to vote for the Russian pairs team .
# text = She later recanted and said that Canadian officials had pressured her .
# text = The ISU later suspended Le Gougne and Gailhaguet for three years .
# text = The federal complaint did not describe the possibility of a wider conspiracy or any contact between Tokhtakhounov , or his unnamed co-conspirators , with Le Gougne .

# text = " We have alleged no connection between this man with any officials other than with Russian federation officials , " James B. Comey , the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York , said at a news conference .
# text = He said that Tokhtakhounov " reached out to a co-conspirator , somebody connected to the Russian Skating Federation , who did the legwork for him . "
# text = Maxwell Miller , Le Gougne 's lawyer in Salt Lake City , said no evidence of organized crime influence came up in her suspension hearings before the ISU
# text = " I think this situation vindicates the argument that we 've made all along , " he said .
# text = " She 's a scapegoat and a target of a corrupt system and was unfairly singled out . "
# text = Tokhtakhounov , whose age was given by Comey as 53 or 62 , is a " major figure in international Eurasian organized crime , " Comey said .
# text = Born in Tashkent , Uzbekistan , and now a Russian citizen , he is known as Taivanchik , or Little Taiwanese , for his Central Asian ethnic background .

# text = Since the collapse of the Soviet Union , he has been implicated in arms trading and Russian art smuggling , and in the Russian news media he was accused of complicity in a plot to extort $ 10 million from the head of a Russian sports foundation .
# text = He appears to have moved to France in 1989 , according to news media reports , and is reported to have Israeli citizenship also .
# text = Comey said Tokhtakhounov had three residences in Italy : Forte dei Marmi , Rome and Milan .

# text = The complaint against Tokhtakhounov 's traces his contact with figure skating to 2000 , when he proposed to Gailhaguet the creation of a professional hockey team in Paris that would provide revenue for the French Skating Federation .
# text = In return , Gailhaguet told the FBI on Feb. 23 as the Olympics were taking place , Tokhtakhounov asked for Gailhaguet 's help in renewing his French visa , which was about to expire .
# text = But when Gailhaguet sought guidance from a French government official , he was told that " Tokhtakhounov 's money is bad , " the affidavit said .
# text = The federal complaint offers many details of the alleged conspiracy , including excerpts from a transcript of the Italian wiretaps .
# text = On Feb. 5 , the Italian wiretaps recorded Tokhtakhounov 's request to someone identified as another Russian mobster to get the number of a Russian Skating Federation official .
# text = The second mobster told Tokhtakhounov that the federation official " is close to us -- he is a good guy , he will do it . "
# text = Tokhtakhounov 's action apparently came soon after he said he received a phone call from the mother of the female ice dancer , presumably Anissina .
# text = A week later , after Berezhnaya and Sikharulidze 's pairs victory , the mobsters spoke again .

# text = The second mobster expressed satisfaction with the outcome of the competition and suggested that Tokhtakhounov could call the ice dancer 's " mother or the father and tell them everything will be OK "
# text = He appears to be referring to Anissina .
# text = The second mobster added , " Our Sikharulidze fell , the Canadians were 10 times better , and in spite of that the French with their vote gave us first place . "
# text = He added : " Everything is going the way you need it . "
# text = They also discussed the coming judging in ice dancing , in which the French and the Italian teams were the favorites .
# text = The second mobster said the French pair had " only three judges , " and of the two judges they needed to win the gold medal " one is ours , and the other our friends will give them . "
# text = Their concern for lining up more votes than they thought the Italian ice dancers had may stem from the Italian team 's defeat of Anissina and Peizerat in the 2001 world championships .
# text = But they seemed pleased that the Russian pair 's victory was achieved with the French judge 's vote .
# text = " The French have nothing but the ice dancing , " the second mobster said .
# text = Again , Tokhtakhounov voiced his need to have his French visa extended , and he said Anissina had tried to help him but Gailhaguet had thwarted her .

# text = Also on Feb. 12 , a week before the ice dancing finals , Tokhtakhounov told Anissina 's mother in a telephone call that the Russian federation official " had called me from America " to assure that " we are going to make " Anissina " an Olympic champion . "
# text = He told her that the Russian skating federation official " will help -- he has two or three judges . "

# text = On or about March 7 , in a conversation between Tokhtakhounov and Anissina , she said she would have won the event without his assistance because the Russian judge did not vote for her and her partner .
# text = She also apologized for not calling to thank him earlier , but that Gailhaguet had forbidden her .
# text = She told Tokhtakhounov that she knew the FBI had interviewed Gailhaguet because of information that Tokhtakhounov " was involved with the results " of the ice dancing .

# text = He assured her that it was nonsense , but that Gailhaguet " knows my name very well -- he tried to help me , and later he made stuff up to scare you so you would not connect me to him even more . "
# text = The conversations seem to indicate a familiarity between Tokhtakhounov and Anissina .
# text = Tass , the official Russian news agency , reported that Anissina attended a ceremony in 1999 at a Paris hotel honoring Tokhtakhounov for his philanthropy .

# text = New York Times News Service

# text = -- IBM opened a sprawling and sophisticated semiconductor factory here on Wednesday that cost more than $ 2.5 billion to build and equip , the largest single capital investment the company has ever made .
# text = The factory , which opens as the computer chip business is in a slump , is a costly and risky move for IBM .

# text = But it is also an expression of confidence by the company that it can remain a technology leader in the highly competitive global semiconductor industry , and a commitment that the best place to execute that strategy is in upstate New York .
# text = IBM is an exception among computer makers in that it still invests heavily in research to advance the design , manufacture and materials used in semiconductor chips .
# text = It is spending more than $ 500 million a year on semiconductor research and development .
# text = The factory will produce a wide range of specialized semiconductors used in everything from the largest mainframe computers to cell phones and video - game consoles .
# text = The new plant is part of IBM 's push to gain a strong lead in chip - making beyond the personal computer business , where Intel and East Asian chip producers hold the advantage .

# text = " The core of our strategy is to lead in technology and attack the high - performance segments of the market , " said John Kelly , senior vice president in charge of IBM 's technology group .
# text = An advantage to having the semiconductor fabricating factory here , Kelly explained , was that it was very close to its research laboratories in nearby Westchester County , N.Y .
# text = To stay ahead in advanced chip technology , he said , moving innovations out of the labs and into the factory as fast as possible is crucial .
# text = " What we call the lab - to - fab time should be as close to zero as possible , " Kelly said .
# text = " If our strategy were anything but to be on the leading edge , we 'd have put the plant in Asia . "
# text = The new factory , which will begin normal production early next year , will employ about 1,000 people .

# text = In remarks during a ribbon - cutting ceremony here on Wednesday , Gov. George E. Pataki said he expected the facility to generate thousands more jobs in the Hudson Valley area for contractors and suppliers catering to the factory .
# text = He praised IBM for being " a critical partner in our economic development efforts " in New York state .
# text = In a brief speech , Samuel J. Palmisano , IBM 's chief executive , emphasized that it was important to make long - term investments despite the current slump in the technology business .
# text = " To play to win in technology , you innovate and you lead , " he said .
# text = But manufacturing technology products is a costly and cyclical business .
# text = In June , IBM announced that it was taking a charge of more than $ 2 billion against earnings .

# text = The largest single reasons for the charge were the cost of getting out of the business of manufacturing hard disks for storage , which it sold to Hitachi , and closing down some of its older semiconductor operations .
# text = But Kelly said the demand for advanced chips , like those produced at IBM 's facility in Burlington , Vt. , is strong .
# text = " I need more capacity in that end of the market , " he said , " and this is factory is critical to meeting that growing demand . "
# text = If IBM has miscalculated the demand , it will suffer badly as both the high operating costs and depreciation on the huge capital investment for the East Fishkill factory drag down earnings .
# text = But industry analysts said the plant should be insulated from a falloff in one or a few segments of the semiconductor market .
# text = The factory is highly automated and designed to shift flexibly to produce many different kinds of chips to suit demand .
# text = " The diversity is the big difference with this plant , " said Richard Doherty , president of Envisioneering , a research firm .
# text = " It gives IBM the capability to make so many different kinds of custom chips , and the world is going to custom chips . "
# text = The 140,000 - square - foot plant is a testament to advanced manufacturing technology .
# text = The 300 - millimeter silicon wafers -- about the size of a standard pizza -- are shuttled around the facility in enclosed plastic pods , which ride on overhead tracks .
# text = They drop down from wires automatically into machines , sheathed in stainless steel and glass , for each stage of processing and fabrication .
# text = Throughout the 500 processing steps , which typically last 20 days , the wafers are not touched by human hands .
# text = The circuits etched into the chips are less than one thousandth the width of a human hair .
# text = Human operators are there to monitor the systems , catch errors and fine-tune the production process for maximum efficiency .

# text = Because each of the hundreds of processing machines is self - enclosed , and essentially airtight , the uniforms operators wear are less constricting than in the previous generation of chip plants , which looked like space suits .
# text = The operators at the East Fishkill factory wear light nylon uniforms , light blue shoe coverings and translucent hair nets made of paper .
# text = They look more like workers in a bakery .
# text = Yes , said Richard Brilla , director of the new facility , " but the donuts are a lot more costly here . "

# text = THE PRODUCE BIN : Bitter melon
# text = The Chinese and Indian varieties differ little in taste .
# text = Though they resemble squashes , they are natives to Asia , rather than the Americas , but are now cultivated in many regions of the world that boast moderate to warm climates .
# text = Hmong farmers grow them in California 's Central Valley , and Mexico has a substantial crop .
# text = Bitter melons can be found in Asian and specialty produce markets primarily from spring through late fall .
# text = Right now , some particularly nice ones are in Bay Area farmers ' markets .
# text = As the gourd ripens , its color changes from near white - pale green to vivid green , often flecked with yellow , and eventually bright orange .
# text = When young , the flavor is relatively mild , with a fresh , sour note .
# text = As it ripens , it gets progressively more bitter due to the quinine it contains .
# text = Bitter melon was selling for 79 cents to $ 1.99 a pound last week .
# text = Bitter melons are used in many Asian cuisines , most prominently Indian , Chinese and Vietnamese .
# text = Generally , they are halved lengthwise , the seeds and fibrous pulp removed and the flesh sliced into crescents .
# text = They are frequently blanched or salted and left to macerate for up to an hour , then rinsed and patted dry to tame the bitterness .
# text = Chinese hot - and - sour soup made with egg white and crabmeat often includes bitter melon .
# text = It also appears in stir - frys , especially those based on pork .
# text = Black bean sauce is a favorite seasoning .
# text = When pickled , bitter melon makes a savory condiment .
# text = In Vietnam , bitter melon halves are stuffed with meat mixtures , such as ground pork with black mushrooms and cellophane noodles , then braised .

# text = Grande dame of cooking still going strong at 90 :
# text = Julia Child celebrates in San Francisco
# text = -- How does it feel to turn 90 and have attained the status of an icon , a living legend ?
# text = " It feels just like it felt before , " Julia Child says with the throaty laugh familiar to millions who cut their culinary teeth on her " French Chef " television series .
# text = While making light of the difference a day -- or another decade -- makes , Child intends to enjoy her birthday thoroughly .

# text = Friday to Sunday , the action moves to Napa , with both members - only and public events at COPIA : The American Center for Wine , Food and the Arts , of which she is an honorary board member .

# text = Aug. 15 , her actual birthday , will see her in Maine at an annual gathering of nieces , nephews , their offspring and friends , who for many years have rolled a joined birthday celebration for several members of the group into a jolly reunion .

# text = The schedule Child and her assistant of 14 years , former pastry chef Stephanie Hersh , have laid out is not exactly a senior - citizen routine , even though Child has always been candid about her age and realistic in assessing her own capabilities .

# text = When the Pasadena native moved back to California from her long - time home in the Boston area last year , she also made the move from a condominium she and her late husband , Paul , had purchased many years ago to a progressive retirement home .
# text = She is in the most active of the four levels available , but should the need arise , she can move on to assisted living facilities within the same complex .
# text = " Julia , " explains Hersh , " made these retirement plans many years ago .
# text = She thinks it 's selfish for people not to make arrangements for their old age in good time . "
# text = But so far , age has been kind to the ebullient Child .

# text = In a phone interview a couple of weeks ago , she reported with glee that surgery early this month to remove a small cyst on her spinal cord had " miraculously " cleared up recent problems in walking : " Turned out there is nothing wrong with my legs at all . "
# text = So she can once again go shopping , buying whatever seems best on any given day .

# text = Though she had a " nice " kitchen installed in her new home , Child said it 's like a ship 's galley -- a far cry from the huge , three - pantry kitchen Paul Child designed for their house in Cambridge .
# text = That may well be the best - known kitchen in America , since it became the site of the " French Chef " television programs , which started airing in 1962 .
# text = " Back there , we always ate in the kitchen , " Child reminisced , " I can not do that here . "
# text = That means her entertaining has been curtailed , even though she still has an active social life with the many friends the Childs made during 22 winters spent in Santa Barbara .
# text = She will have reunions of sorts with her famous kitchen in the next few weeks .

# text = One of its Peg - Board walls was dismantled and reinstalled at COPIA ; the rest went to Washington , D.C. , and the Behring Center of the Smithsonian Institution 's National Museum of American History .
# text = Hersh recalls the museum staff 's approach to preserving the famous kitchen as awesome : They cataloged and photographed everything , from stove to windows , blinds to drawer contents .
# text = As reinstalled in Washington , the kitchen should be as we all remember it from countless TV shows , " right down to the toothpicks . "
# text = Child will go to the capital for the debut of the exhibit right after the Maine birthday bash .
# text = To see her kitchen -- and by extension , herself -- enshrined in the Smithsonian , she said , " will be an odd feeling " and no doubt bring back memories .
# text = But Child is not one to get maudlin about the past , though she does want to keep it alive .
# text = She 's already got her next project picked out : A memoir of her and Paul 's life in the diplomatic service with his professional photographs and some of her collected recipes .

# text = So what do you prepare when asked to cook a birthday dinner for America 's most famous culinary personality ?

# text = RESPONSIBLE SEAFOOD SALES ARE THE CATCH OF THE DAY
# text = ATTENTION EDITORS : This article from the NEWHOUSE NEWS SERVICE report of TUESDAY , JULY 30 , 2002 , is available as a " separate buy . "
# text = For information about purchasing the article , contact DEBRA WEYDERT of The New York Times Syndicate at 732-390-4480 ; fax , 732-390-4697 ; e-mail , weyded-LRB-at-RRB-nytimes.com
# text = Chefs and seafood retailers are wading into one of the hottest natural resource issues of the day : fisheries management .

# text = It 's no longer unusual for chefs to refuse to serve a species they think to be at risk of extinction or for a retailer to promote seafoods that are abundant and part of a healthy marine ecosystem .
# text = Most say they 're driven by the desire to do right by the environment .
# text = Some also say they must listen to their customers ' concerns or risk a consumer backlash .
# text = The nationwide boycott of Chilean seabass is a potent example of the new activism .
# text = " I have made it a policy of mine never to serve Chilean seabass , " said Billy Hahn , executive chef at Jake 's Famous Crawfish , a Portland , Ore. , landmark since 1892 .
# text = " I refuse to sell it . "
# text = Chilean seabass , also known as Patagonian toothfish , came into vogue in the 1990s in U.S. restaurants and fish markets .
# text = With rising demand for the firm , oil - rich fish came pirate fishing fleets eager to cash in on its popularity -- even if it meant skirting catch limits and environmental regulations .
# text = Contrary to what some restaurants and retailers tell their customers , the U.S. government does not consider the Chilean seabass to be endangered .
# text = But in some areas , the seabass are being overfished .

# text = That is potentially a problem because Chilean seabass are a long - lived species -- living as long as 50 years -- and reproduce slowly , said Susan Buchanan , a spokeswoman for the federal government 's National Marine Fisheries Service .
# text = The NMFS estimates that in 2000 , more than 16,000 tons of Chilean seabass were legally caught from an internationally regulated harvest area in the Antarctic Ocean .
# text = But more than 32,000 tons may have been taken illegally from those same waters , the fisheries service said .
# text = Impatient with regulators , the National Environmental Trust began a boycott campaign in February called " Take a Pass on Chilean Seabass . "
# text = The Washington - based conservation group says more than 530 restaurants have signed on .
# text = A number of restaurants not officially part of the National Environmental Trust boycott also have stopped serving Chilean seabass .
# text = And it 's not just the white tablecloth crowd .

# text = Red Lobster , with 660 restaurants in the United States and Canada , dropped Chilean seabass from the menu in the past year because of " sustainability " concerns , said Wendy Spirduso , communications director for the Orlando , Fla. - based chain .
# text = Some retailers also have pulled Chilean seabass .
# text = " We 've discontinued selling swordfish , Chilean seabass , orange roughy and marlin , " said Mark Cockcroft , national seafood buyer for Wild Oats Markets , a chain of 103 stores .
# text = " We are also taking a real hard look currently at almost all species of shark , though we have n't made a formal statement about that . "
# text = Whole Foods Markets , with 133 stores nationwide , also does not sell Chilean seabass .

# text = All of this comes at a time when Americans are consuming more seafood : 15 to 16 pounds per person each year , compared with 10.3 pounds per person in 1960 and 12.5 pounds in 1980 , according to the National Fisheries Institute , an industry association .
# text = At the same time , about half the world 's fisheries are being fished to capacity .

# text = The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations reports that 47 percent to 50 percent of stocks are " fully exploited , " meaning that catches have either reached or are close to maximum limits .
# text = Another 15 percent to 18 percent are " overexploited , " and 9 percent to 10 percent have been " depleted or are recovering from depletion .
# text = " The seafood industry is less than thrilled about this surge of interest in ocean ecosystems from people who are not scientists .
# text = Fisheries management is best left to the experts , said Thor Lassen , president of Ocean Trust , a research and conservation foundation partly financed by the fishing industry .
# text = " It involves very complicated choices that have to do with the biology of species , their life cycles , how they respond to various changes in the oceans , etc. "
# text = When there 's a boycott , Lassen said , " it 's not environmentalists or chefs making the sacrifice , it 's coastal communities . "
# text = Rod Moore , executive director of the West Coast Seafood Processors Association , suggests that activists with an agenda are manipulating chefs and retailers .

# text = The conservation groups providing information to chefs and retailers and lists of environmentally appropriate seafoods to consumers are the same groups working to affect fisheries management on the political and regulatory level , Moore said .
# text = That 's simply good strategy , said James Leape , deputy director of the conservation program for the David and Lucile Packard Foundation in Los Altos , Calif .
# text = In 2000 and 2001 , the Packard Foundation awarded $ 26 million in marine fisheries conservation grants .
# text = They included support for marine reserves and money for fisheries management reform .
# text = More than $ 7 million was given to projects aimed at educating the general public .

# text = " One of the principal concerns of the Packard Foundation is the preservation of natural resources , particularly in the oceans , and one of the greatest threats is overfishing , " Leape said .
# text = " We have seen that raising consumer awareness and concern among restaurants and retailers about a particular fishery can really make a difference . " "
# text = The Monterey Bay Aquarium 's Web site rates different species of fish for overfishing , habitat damage and other factors .
# text = The California aquarium also created " Seafood Watch " wallet cards designed to take to restaurants .
# text = More than 600,000 of the cards and seafood guides have been distributed since 2000 , said Jennifer Dianto , Seafood Watch program manager at the aquarium .
# text = Chefs and retailers around the country know they must be prepared to deal with customers who arrive with the aquarium 's seafood card in hand .
# text = But in a business in which 12 - hour shifts are the norm , some chefs worry about their lack of time to stay informed about complicated , rapidly changing fisheries management issues .
# text = Some working chefs say they routinely review conservation group Web sites , government reports and industry sources .
# text = " For me , it 's very difficult to be certain that the information which is given to me is real , " said Eric Ripert , chef at Le Bernardin , a four - star seafood restaurant in Manhattan .
# text = I do n't have enough information to know , for example , if Chilean seabass is really disappearing or if it 's political pressure . "
# text = Despite being uncertain of its status , Ripert pulled Chilean seabass .
# text = Le Bernardin 's menu also informs diners that the restaurant will not serve swordfish to support efforts " to recover the species . "
# text = " I do n't wish to be a spokesman for any campaign , " Ripert said .
# text = " I do it as somebody who has a conscience and is caring . "

# text = PRESCRIPTION PRIVILEGES MAKE SOME PSYCHOLOGISTS ANXIOUS

# text = Intending to ease consumer access to mental health care , New Mexico legislators in March passed a law allowing psychologists to prescribe psychotropic medications , such as antidepressants .

# text = But powerful groups , including the American Medical Association , oppose the idea and have a surprising source of support : psychologists themselves , some of whom call it a radical experiment and fear that the most likely victim will be the science of psychology .

# text = " I am concerned that nonmedically trained people as legitimate prescribers of drugs will not be accepted by the American public , " says psychologist Gerald C. Davison of the University of Southern California .
# text = The APA has spent more than $ 1 million to help state psychological associations develop and lobby for such prescription privileges -- or " RxP " -- legislation .
# text = A total of 31 state psychology associations have task forces dedicated to developing and lobbying for prescription - privileges legislation .

# text = The version endorsed by the APA would license doctoral - level psychologists to independently prescribe psychotropic drugs after completing 300 hours of classroom instruction in neuroscience , physiology and pharmacology , followed by four months ' supervised treatment of 100 patients .

# text = Critics say that is not nearly enough compared with other prescribers , such as M.D. psychiatrists or nurse practitioners who have at least six years ' medical education and clinical experience .
# text = Neither Davison nor most other RxP opponents doubt the efficacy of medications .
# text = Their greatest objection is to the notion of turning psychology into a prescribing profession .

# text = In a field that has struggled long and hard to prove that mind , mood and behavior can be studied empirically , the past decade , Davison says , has seen " exciting developments " that demonstrate the validity of various psychotherapeutic interventions and the psychosocial - behavioral models on which they are based .

# text = " The timing is peculiar to abandon psychological science or to convert it to a medical science , " explains Elaine M. Heiby of the University of Hawaii , who chairs a committee of the 1,000 - member American Association of Applied and Preventive Psychology that is concerned about the medicalization of psychology .
# text = More than any philosophical betrayal of psychology , RxP opponents fear that the movement will undermine the science they love .

# text = They believe that if prescriptive authority becomes the norm , biomedical requirements will inevitably seep into the psychology curriculum , at the expense of traditional psychological science and methodology .
# text = Lilienfeld feels that many clinical psychologists already receive inadequate training in fundamentals such as research design and evaluation .
# text = RxP opponents charge the APA with pushing its prescription - privileges agenda without adequately assessing support for it in the field .
# text = The 300 - member SSCP is the only group within the APA to have taken a formal stance against prescription privileges .
# text = The APA has scheduled 30 minutes at its meeting in August for an RxP debate , but its leadership believes it already has an accurate sense of support for its RxP policy .
# text = " Except for this small vocal minority , we have just not gotten a lot of groundswell against this from members , " says APA president Philip G. Zimbardo of Stanford University .
# text = With prescription privileges now a reality in one state , some RxP opponents concede that it may be too late .
# text = This year four states besides New Mexico -- Georgia , Hawaii , Illinois and Tennessee -- have pending legislation for psychologist prescription privileges .
# text = Over the past decade , 14 state legislatures have considered such laws .

# text = Between 1991 and 1997 , a U.S. Department of Defense psychopharmacology demonstration project involving two to four years ' training produced 10 military psychologists who can write prescriptions .

# text = A mission to end a war
# text = -- Tom Karnes was dialing for destiny , but not everyone wanted to cooperate .
# text = Karnes sat in his wood - paneled office in a Quonset hut in the middle of the Great Salt Lake Desert , a black telephone to his ear .
# text = He was tracking down men to join a group so secret he could n't admit it existed .
# text = On his metal desk were names of military men being ordered into the organization .
# text = He was calling bases all over the United States to line up their transfer to the desert outside Salt Lake City .
# text = " Where is the authority ? " asked one officer who did n't want to lose a valuable man under his command .
# text = " Who says this ? " another commanding officer asked Karnes .
# text = Each time , Karnes said what he had to : " Call Air Force headquarters if you do n't believe me . "
# text = If they continued to resist , he pulled out a secret code for their bosses .
# text = " This is a Silverplate request , " he said .
# text = Silverplate : code word for the historic mission that would end World War II .
# text = Almost 1,800 men were assembled n late 1944 to join the top - secret unit called the 509th Composite Group .
# text = Col. Paul Tibbets , the pilot who would drop the world 's first atomic bomb over Hiroshima , Japan , was commander of the unit and chose the men .
# text = And the first person he chose to join him was Karnes , though he could n't reveal the mission to Karnes .
# text = Karnes , 87 , is a retired history professor who lives in suburban Austin with his wife , Virginia , who also worked for the 509th as a civilian bookkeeper for six months .

# text = Karnes was Tibbets ' adjutant , the man in charge of writing the orders and cajoling the transfer to the unit of servicemen proficient in bombing , mechanics , ordnance , engineering and communications .
# text = Tibbets picked the names , and Karnes made it happen .
# text = Karnes thought it was a breeze .
# text = They were a wartime match that changed the world .
# text = Japan surrendered within days of the detonation of the atomic bombs that killed 140,000 people in Hiroshima on Aug. 6 , 1945 , and 70,000 in Nagasaki three days later .

# text = The story of the 509th is a tale of an elite outfit that lived in a bubble of secrecy and endured the taunts of other war - weary U.S. units that resented sharing a small Pacific island with the 509th , which appeared exempt from combat .
# text = Tinian Island was the staging area where the 509th moved after its creation in the desert .
# text = Karnes has never spoken publicly about his role as Tibbets ' right - hand administrative aide .
# text = He never even told his story to students in his 40 years of teaching college .
# text = War is hell , he says , and when it was over , he wanted to come home and rejoin his young family and not dwell on it .
# text = He earned a doctorate in history from Stanford University and taught Latin American history at Tulane University and Arizona State University .
# text = Next week marks the 57th anniversary of the atomic bombings .
# text = As always , Karnes ' mind will drift to memories of his good friend Tibbets , 87 , who lives in Columbus , Ohio .
# text = Each year on Aug. 6 , " I always think of Paul Tibbets and how he handled unbelievable responsibility , " Karnes said .
# text = Karnes met Tibbets when the 29 - year - old bomber pilot walked into Karnes ' office at Wendover Army Air Field on the Utah - Nevada border .
# text = Karnes was the personnel and classification officer .
# text = He was only a captain , but he had been left in charge at Wendover the day Tibbets surprised them by landing a B-29 , a new plane no one at Wendover had seen .
# text = Tibbets had just been ordered to organize a combat force to drop a bomb being developed by a secret enterprise known as the Manhattan Project .
# text = He was searching for a remote installation to train bomber crews and support units in total secrecy .
# text = Tibbets instantly liked the isolation and vast size of Wendover and the surrounding Bonneville Salt Flats .
# text = And he immediately liked Karnes , who showed him around the base .
# text = In Karnes , Tibbets found a kindred spirit -- and a handball partner .
# text = Both were smart , disciplined , quiet men who thrived on efficiency , perfection and self - reliance .
# text = Each had skills the other admired .
# text = Tibbets was a decorated , top - gun pilot , but Karnes could wrangle the military rule book as well as Tibbets could fly .
# text = " I do n't recall ever having to tell Tom to do anything , " Tibbets said in an e-mail this week .
# text = " He was so knowledgeable he just got things done , allowing me to concentrate on other matters .
# text = I was very lucky to have Tom . "
# text = Tibbets quickly returned to Wendover after that first visit to set up his headquarters .
# text = His first order appointed Karnes adjutant for the 509th .
# text = Almost overnight , Wendover became a high - security base filled with off - limit areas covered in barbed wire .
# text = No one was allowed to talk about what they saw or heard , even though most of the 509th had no idea why they were there , except that 15 B-29s were being modified to carry a heavy load .
# text = Karnes and his staff read outgoing mail to make sure no secrets slipped out .
# text = Karnes hated to pry , and skimmed over personal portions of the letters .
# text = Karnes knew the 509th was preparing for a special bombing mission , but he had no idea what kind of bombs were involved .
# text = " I had a friend , the finance officer .
# text = He said that they had split the atom and that we were going to drop an atomic bomb , " Karnes said .

column1: # text = By spring , the 509th prepared to move to Tinian Island , near Guam and Saipan .
# text = That would put the B-29s about 1,500 miles from Japan -- a 13 - hour round - trip flight .
# text = Karnes was deluged with orders for inoculations , equipment , transfers and promotions .
# text = Karnes arrived on Tinian on May 18 , 1945 , as part of an advance team that flew in the five C-54 transport planes of the 509th .
# text = On May 29 , 1,200 men arrived on the troopship Cape Victory after a five - week trip from Seattle .
# text = Tinian Island had been captured from Japan , and the Seabees , the construction arm of the Navy , had built two large airfields .
# text = The 509th took North Field and stayed in relative isolation from other B-29 units on the island .
# text = Karnes handed out bunk assignments , choosing the mess officer , Chuck Perry , to share his tent .
# text = Karnes had his own Jeep , and went to the beach and to evening movies shown by other units as often as he could .
# text = But at the movies , he had to remove the distributor cap on his Jeep so the vehicle would n't be stolen , perhaps by jealous airmen who resented the 509th .
# text = Not until the day before Tibbets and his crew flew to Hiroshima was the 509th told what was happening .
# text = The word spread : " This is it .
# text = This is the big mission . "
# text = Karnes and hundreds of other men from the 509th stood along the flight line as Tibbets and the Enola Gay took off at 2:45 a.m. on Aug. 6 , a warm , tropical night .
# text = Three B-29s had gone ahead to check the weather at Hiroshima and two other possible bomb sites .
# text = Two other B-29s left in two - minute intervals after Tibbets so their crews could take photos and drop devices to measure radiation and other effects of the bomb .
# text = Tibbets got the word only an hour from Hiroshima that the city 's weather was clear .
# text = As they approached , Tibbets braced for Japanese anti-aircraft fire .
# text = Early in the flight , the crew had inserted a plug of uranium into the 9,000 - pound bomb , nicknamed " Little Boy . "
# text = Ninety seconds from the bomb drop , Tibbets put the plane on auto-pilot .
# text = The crew slipped on dark glasses to prepare for the blinding flash of the bomb .
# text = At 8:15 a.m. Hiroshima time , the pneumatic bomb - bay doors opened and " Little Boy , " equivalent to 20,000 tons of TNT , fell out .
# text = Tibbets and his crew had exactly 43 seconds to get away before the bomb exploded .
# text = The Enola Gay climbed , and Tibbets fought to turn the plane in the air - bending , 155 - degree the crews had been practicing off Tinian for months .
# text = He pushed off the dark glasses because he could n't see to fly .
# text = When the bomb exploded as planned 1,890 feet over Hiroshima , Tibbets ' mouth tingled , and he tasted the lead fillings in his teeth .
# text = A minute later , the shock wave hit .
# text = The crew was horrified by the purple mushroom cloud that climbed to 10 miles and looked as if it would engulf the Enola Gay .
# text = More shocking was the city of Hiroshima , which was on fire and bubbling like tar .
# text = " We were all appalled , " the pilot said in his book " The Tibbets Story . "
# text = Back on Tinian , Karnes had gone to bed .
# text = But he did n't sleep long .
# text = Arnold told Karnes , " Tibbets is going to be landing in three to four hours , and I want to give him the Distinguished Service Cross , and it is your job to write up the explanation . "
# text = " I had no idea how you wrote up an award .
# text = I 'd never written up any award , " Karnes said .

# text = When an unsuspecting Tibbets descended from the Enola Gay on Tinian , he barely managed to palm his pipe as Gen. Carl Spaatz , commander of the Strategic Air Forces , stepped forward to pin the medal on his bomb flight coveralls .
# text = Karnes , like the hundreds of others gathered along the flight line , was jubilant .
# text = He knew the war would soon be over and he would be heading home .
# text = Three days later , another B-29 from the 509th bombed Nagasaki .
# text = Five days later , Japan surrendered and World War II was over .
# text = Today , Karnes is frustrated that some of his fellow historians , the ones he calls " revisionists , " question the wisdom and morality of the bombings .
# text = What matters , he believes , is that his generation thought the bomb should be dropped .
# text = " We were not bloodthirsty guys , " he said .
# text = " We were convinced then , and I still am , that we ended the war a year or two earlier .
# text = And what the casualties would have been , who knows -- but heavy . "
# text = " On Tinian , and probably elsewhere , the Seabees were building enormous hospitals while we were there , " he said .
# text = " Those hospitals were not for us .
# text = And then the casualties were going to be terrible . "
# text = Karnes carries the image of hundreds of hospital beds in his mind .
# text = In his heart , he holds the unshakable conviction that the mission he helped organize saved America from disaster .
