# text = Details are a major preoccupation of the architect .
# text = The function of a baseboard is to cover the joint between the wall and the floor , and secondarily to protect the wall from scuffing .
# text = There are dozens of ways that this can be done .
# text = Baseboards can be prominent or discreet , a complicated assembly of board , cap and base , or a simple strip of hardwood .
# text = Or nothing ? many modern architects dispense with baseboards altogether .
# text = The baseboards in my living room are twelve inches tall .
# text = They are not wood but cast iron , since they are really disguised radiators .

# text = My house was built in 1908 , influenced by the British Free Style of Voysey and Baillie Scott , and to further preserve a simple , rustic atmosphere the architect had the baseboards $$ radiators painted to resemble wood .

# text = Railings have a simple function ? they must be sturdy enough to support us if we lean on them , and they must provide a secure hand - hold : if railings are open , the spaces between the supports and the rails should be small enough to prevent children from falling through .
# text = Classical railings , developed during the Renaissance , consist of balusters supporting a handrail .
# text = Balusters ? little columns ? can have a single or a double swelling curve , or a vase shape .
# text = Fabricated in wood or masonry , they can be round or square in cross - section , and plain or highly ornamented .
# text = Railings can be replaced by parapets with pierced screens .
# text = These can be stone or metal : bronze , wrought , or cast iron .
# text = The screens can be simple X - shapes , intertwining geometrical patterns , or complicated floral figures as in Art Nouveau staircases .
# text = Perhaps the simplest open railings are those of the great Adirondack camps , whose builders mimicked X - shaped wrought - iron railings in unpeeled rustic tree trunks .
# text = Modern railings are usually metal .

# text = In his early villas , Le Corbusier used white - painted pipe railings to create a nautical image ; in later buildings like the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts at Harvard , flat steel bars take the place of pipes .

# text = The railings in Mies van der Rohe RSQUOs buildings usually have only a single intermediate rail , located precisely halfway between the handrail and the floor ; the vertical stanchions , the handrail , and the rail are made of identical square steel bars .
# text = The railings in Louis Kahn buildings tend to be parapets , but where he is obliged to use an open railing the design is as simple as possible .
# text = I have seen a short stair railing that consisted of a single bronze bar , bent at each end to form the uprights .
# text = Richard Meier uses metal railings , too , but because there are sometimes as many as six horizontal rails , the visual effect is more pronounced ? they resemble staffs in sheet music .

# text = When Brutalism was in fashion , railings were correspondingly heavy : concrete beams , wide enough to sit on but unpleasant to the touch , or massive wood balustrades , as solid as fenders on a truck dock .
# text = The vogue among many younger architects today is toward lightness and exposed construction , and railings reflect that fashion , too .

# text = The screens of the railings of Peter Rose RSQUOs Canadian Center for Architecture in Montreal are industrial - looking perforated sheets of anodized aluminum , prominently bolted to the stanchions .
# text = These solutions appear mannered compared to the simple railing that I. M. Pei designed for the East Building of the National Gallery .

# text = The stainless steel handrail highlights the solidity of the rose - colored Tennessee marble by appearing to float in mid-air , since it is supported by continuous sheets of tempered glass embedded in the floor .
# text = The transparent railings of I. M. Pei RSQUOs East Building are understated , elegant , and luxurious ? like the building .
# text = The successful relationship of the details to each other , and to the building is governed by the architect RSQUOs sense of style .

# text = That is why the architect of my house painted the radiators to resemble wood ; a technologically inclined architect might have painted them silver ; a minimalist would dispense with baseboards and hide the radiators in the wall .
# text = The role of details is not to complement architecture ; details are architecture .
# text = Mies van der Rohe is supposed to have said " God is in the details . "
# text = He meant that details are the soul of architecture .

# text = That is why , just as an archaeologist can reconstruct a pot from a few shards , or a paleontologist can surmise the form of a prehistoric animal from bone fragments , it is possible to divine the architect RSQUOs idea of a building by examining its details .
# text = The house that Robert Venturi built for his mother in 1964 shook the foundations of the International Style ; much of this effect was the result of details .

# text = Although Venturi obviously was working in a Modernist idiom ? there is a strip window and a steel - pipe railing ? he also incorporated distinctly un-Modernist features such as trim , both inside and out .
# text = Classical architects use a large variety of moldings ? fillet , astragal , egg and dart , ogee ? that can be combined and recombined to great decorative effect .
# text = The International Style , in its effort to do away with ornament , outlawed trim .
# text = Joints between materials were simply hairline cracks .

# text = The conspicuous exterior dado , the baseboards , and the chair - rails in the Vanna Venturi House were hardly Classical moldings ? they were merely boards with chamfered edges ? yet they challenged the assumption that trim and Modernism were incompatible .
# text = Coming through the front door of the Vanna Venturi House one immediately senses that it is an unusual place .
# text = A broad stair rises beside the fireplace , then peters out to almost nothing .
# text = The fireplace looks like an abstract sculpture , but it has a traditional mantelpiece .
# text = A free - standing column à la Corbusier stands beside a chair - rail .
# text = Then there is the furniture .
# text = Ever since the Tugendhat House ? for which Mies had designed the furniture ? it was taken for granted that modern houses required modern furniture .
# text = Instead of the iconic bent - tube Breuer chairs , there are homely ladderback chairs around the dining table ; instead of an Eames lounge chair and ottoman , a comfortable stuffed sofa .
# text = It is a contradictory atmosphere ? the International Style willfully distorted through the lens of traditional bourgeois domesticity .

# text = Whether one is looking up at the tall dome of the Pantheon , descending the spiraling vortex of Wright RSQUOs Guggenheim Museum , or standing in the living room of Venturi RSQUOs small house , the experience of architecture is above all the experience of being in a separate , distinct world .
# text = That is what distinguishes architecture from sculpture ? it is not an object but a place .
# text = The sense of being in a special place that is a three - dimensional expression of the architect RSQUOs imagination is one of the distinctive pleasures of architecture .
# text = To create a strong sense of place , the surroundings must be all of a piece ; space , mass , shapes , and materials must reflect the same sensibility .
# text = That is why details are so important .
# text = A jarring detail or an inconsistency ? something " out of place " ? and the fantasy begins to crumble .
# text = Illusion has been a part of architecture ever since the ancient Greeks made columns with a gently swelling taper to deceive the eye .
# text = This is not to say that architecture is stage décor .
# text = When the wind blows , the canvas scenery blows over ; the building resists the elements .
# text = Architecture surrounds and shelters us .
# text = It is the real world but it is also a vision .

# text = ??? The Postmodern movement that followed the Vanna Venturi House was relatively short - lived but it had an important consequence : it broke the stranglehold of Modernism , leaving designers free to explore other forms of expression .
# text = The profusion of styles that ensued is demonstrated by the work of three gifted but vastly different architects , Allan Greenberg , Hugh Newell Jacobsen , and Enrique Norten .
# text = Allan Greenberg is a confirmed Classicist .
# text = He does not consider this an anomaly .
# text = " To be truly modern , " he writes , " means finding the dynamic balance between eternal human values and the specific demands of the present .
# text = Although Greenberg looks to the past , his is not the attitude of an archeologist .
# text = Like Carrère & Hastings , and generations of architects before them , Greenberg approaches Classicism as a tradition to be studied , absorbed ? then extended .

# text = Early in his career , after emigrating to the United States from South Africa , Greenberg was employed writing design standards for courthouses , which led to an unusual commission : the conversion of an empty supermarket into a courthouse .
# text = He gave the commercial building in Manchester , Connecticut , a new façade dominated by a large arch , over-scaled voussoirs , and a pediment .
# text = Inside , the barrel - vaulted ceiling of the lobby was supported by a Tuscan order .
# text = Greenberg had graduated from Yale in 1965 , and like many of his contemporaries was experimenting with the new freedom offered by Postmodernism .
# text = However , unlike Venturi and Moore , Greenberg was not coyly introducing Classical elements into a Modernist building ; he was returning to Classical roots .

# text = From this modest beginning , over the next two decades , came a variety of commissions : a suite of rooms for the Secretary of State in the United States Department of State building , several college and university buildings , and a Roman Catholic church .

# text = His commercial work included a newspaper office building in Athens , Georgia , a new entrance for Bergdorf Goodman on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan , and a flagship store for Tommy Hilfiger in Beverly Hills .
# text = Greenberg is also known for large country houses , both in the United States and in Europe .
# text = Like Lutyens and John Russell Pope , he ventures stylistically farther afield in his residential work ? using Georgian and American Colonial styles .
# text = One of his early houses was inspired by Mount Vernon , another by Palladio RSQUOs unfinished Villa Thiene .
# text = Several are picturesque rambling affairs whose relaxed informality recalls the best work of McKim , Mead & White .
# text = One of my favorite Greenberg houses is a cottage set among windblown dunes on the eastern seaboard .
# text = Completed in 1992 , the low - lying building is shingled , but it is not exactly Shingle Style .
# text = Recent Shingle Style buildings are often broken down into many small parts , giving them a fussy and nervous appearance .
# text = Such seaside cottages look as if a good wind could blow them away .
# text = Greenberg RSQUOs aim here is to make a heavyweight building of great solidity that is rooted firmly in the dune scrub .
# text = The one - story Atlantic façade is almost perfectly symmetrical : a large arched window flanked by two semi-circular bays , rotund sentinels standing against the ocean winds .
# text = The two - story landward side is more informal , ringed by a sheltered porch .
# text = Massivity informs the details : sturdy Tuscan columns , a heavy cornice at the eaves of the large roof , rugged window frames .
# text = The sense of robustness is accentuated by occasional delicacy : the arched window incorporates scrolled brackets that support an elegant reverse ogee molding at the eaves .
# text = Inside , the fireplace has a brick hearth , a slate lintel , and a wood surround , whose almost modern simplicity is softened by a cavetto molding beneath the mantelpiece .
# text = The ceiling is supported by exposed trusses of rough , reused timbers .
# text = Although most people would describe this house as " traditional , " this is not an exercise in a particular historical style .
# text = There is a nod here to the British Arts and Crafts architect C. F. A. Voysey , and it is obvious that Greenberg has looked at Lutyens ? country houses .
# text = But this is a modern house , although designed by an architect with a Classical sensibility .
# text = It admirably fulfills Palladio RSQUOs call for a correspondence of the whole with the parts and the parts with the whole .
# text = Hugh Newell Jacobsen studied at Yale under Louis Kahn , worked for Philip Johnson , and opened his own office in 1958 .
# text = He established himself as a premier residential architect , winning commissions in the United States and abroad and receiving numerous design awards .
# text = Several of the awards were for restoration of historic buildings , notably the Renwick Gallery in Washington , D.C. , and the Hôtel Talleyrand in Paris .
# text = A Modernist by training and inclination , Jacobsen was , nevertheless , affected by the winds of change unleashed by Venturi RSQUOs little house .
# text = Starting in 1980 , he evolved a hybrid style in which American regional forms and materials are combined with International Style precision , spareness , and simplicity .

# text = A house on Nantucket in shingles and white trim looks vernacular until one notices the careful proportions and refined , elegant details such as tall French doors in the living room that slide into wall pockets that also conceal shutters and screen doors .
# text = A post - and - beam Caribbean guest house with broad overhangs has the ingenuous simplicity of a beach shack .
# text = The Palladian plan and temple - like pavilions of an Ohio residence pay homage to the local Greek Revival .
# text = An Ohio country house recalls a board - and - batten Gothic Revival farmhouse .
# text = The Palmedo House , built in 1988 , reinterprets the American Colonial architecture of its location ? Long Island .
# text = At first glance , the six pavilions resemble a little village , a little Amish village , judging from the austere white wood siding , the prim details , and the identical pitched roofs .
# text = This sounds precious , but Jacobsen is not a romantic .
# text = The central " house " contains the living room , a three - story space open to the roof .

# text = Although the multi-paned windows are present at an upper level of the wall , the corner of the room is glazed with large , mullionless sheets of plate glass , offering dramatic views of Long Island Sound .
# text = This is an International Style device , as is the economy of detail and the clean , cool , atmosphere of the interior .

# text = On the other hand , the fireplace , which in an orthodox International Style house would be painted brick or bush - hammered concrete , is decorously built into the wall , which gives the room a traditional , civilized air .
# text = The chief idea here is to highlight the tension between old and new , between the traditional clapboarded architecture and the demands of modern life .
# text = Whereas Greenberg seamlessly resolves this tension , Jacobsen allows it to surface .
# text = If this sounds like textbook Postmodernism , it is not .
# text = Jacobsen artlessly combines new and old without the slightest hint of irony .
# text = Jacobsen reacts to the collapse of Modernism by seeking a compromise position , while Greenberg anchors himself in the certainties of Classicism .
# text = Enrique Norten , the youngest of the three , takes a different course ? he is trying to put Modernism back together again .
# text = Norten , who studied at Cornell , established his office in his native Mexico City in 1985 .
# text = In a relatively short time he produced an impressive body of work that includes institutional , commercial , and residential buildings .
# text = His major projects are a services building for the media giant TELEVISA and the National School of Theater .
# text = Both incorporate bulging , metal shell - roofs that recall the 1950s buildings of the French architect - engineer Jean Prouvé .
# text = Prouvé was intent on applying new methods of construction , particularly industrialization and prefabrication .
# text = His buildings , extremely light and assembled from standardized elements , were real " machines for living . "
# text = Norten , too , is preoccupied with industrial building technologies , the lighter the better .
# text = Double - tensed glass curtain walls are mysteriously supported by a steel - frame .
# text = Roofs hang by steel cables from steel masts .
# text = Slender , canted columns brace a glass - roofed portico .
# text = Railings , in a Norten design , are almost always opportunities for structural legerdemain : suspended sheets of glass , stretched steel cables , perforated metal screens .
# text = In 1994 , Norten built a house for himself and his family on a tight urban site in Mexico City .
# text = The three - story street façade is mostly a blank concrete wall ; the wall facing the interior walled patio is entirely glass .
# text = The main living floor is open , except for the kitchen ; the upper bedroom floor is shaded and given privacy by a redwood , louvered screen .
# text = A functionalist style pervades the house .
# text = The clinical cabinetwork is white - painted wood .
# text = A concrete wall in the dining room is bare save for the regular pattern of the formwork ties and the pour lines marks .
# text = The windows are large sections of plate glass in simple aluminum frames ; a 10 - foot section slides aside to entirely open the dining room to the patio .
# text = The sliding wall recalls the disappearing windows in Mies van der Rohe RSQUOs Tugendhat House , but the resemblance ends here .
# text = Mies ? spare interior is opulent and assertive ; Norten RSQUOs is austere , almost monastic : a neutral background for family life .
# text = This is an unsentimental idea of the home .
# text = Not exactly a " machine for living , " but certainly machinelike in its precision and rational layout .
# text = Like Greenberg and Jacobsen , Norten reflects on the past .

# text = Although his house has little to do formally with the International Style of the flat - roofed stucco villas of the 1920s ? except for the white - painted circular steel columns ? it shares that period RSQUOs ambitions ; it is highly abstract , idealistic , technophile , and lacking in applied ornament .

# text = Decoration results not from trim , but from the surface quality of the different materials ? concrete , red oak flooring , etched glass - and from the relentless articulation of structural connections .
# text = Norten RSQUOs buildings exhibit another feature of the International Style : they are placeless .
# text = That is , while they carefully respond to the specifics of the program and the site , they do not explicitly acknowledge their immediate regional context .
# text = Whether they are in Mexico or New Mexico ? where Norten is building a heritage center ? the style is the same : understated , coolly competent , cosmopolitan .
# text = The buildings are different , yet the three architects have something in common .
# text = They are serious about what they are doing , that is , their buildings exhibit a strong sense of conviction .
# text = They pay enormous attention to details .
# text = They are disciplined , but they understand their self - imposed rules well enough to occasionally break them .
# text = Moreover , while their architecture is built with a great sense of style , it is never merely stylized .
# text = That is because in their buildings , style ? the manner of expression ? is always in the service of content ? that which is being expressed .
# text = Style without content quickly degenerates into caricature , like a speaker who makes grand gestures and rhetorical flourishes , but has nothing to say .
# text = The buildings of Greenberg , Jacobsen , and Norten , on the contrary , have a great deal to tell us about our past , our surroundings , and ourselves .
# text = Greenberg , Jacobsen , and Norten do not describe what they do in terms of style .
# text = I think that there are a number of reasons that architects are uncomfortable talking about the subject .

# text = A suspicion of style is a heritage of the Modern Movement , which preached against the arbitrary dictates of style and fashion , while maintaining an unspoken but rigid stylistic consistency .
# text = So deep - rooted is this teaching that it remains a moral stricture on most architects , whether or not they are Modernists .
# text = Perhaps another reason for the reluctance to discuss style is fear .
# text = Fear that being linked to a particular style is to be put in a box ? like most creative people , architects dislike being categorized .
# text = Also fear that talking about style will make architecture ? a serious business ? sound frivolous .
# text = Better to leave that to interior decorators and fashion designers , professions that architects regard with a mixture of disdain and envy .
# text = Finally , there is an unspoken fear of style because it is subject to the whims and the fancies of fashion .
# text = That fear , at least , seems to me to be ill - founded .
# text = An architecture that recognizes style ? and fashion ? would not be an architecture that is introspective and self - referential , as are so many contemporary buildings .
# text = It would be part of the world ? not architecture for architects , but architecture for the rest of us .
# text = And that would not be a bad thing .
# text = Richard Morris Hunt was the most celebrated American architect of the late nineteenth century .

# text = His preeminence is reflected by his appointment as the architect of two important national works : the centerpiece building of the Chicago World RSQUOs Columbian Exposition , and the pedestal for the Statue of Liberty .
# text = He was feted at home and abroad .

# text = Hunt was the first architect to receive an honorary doctorate from Harvard and the first American to receive a Gold Medal from the Royal Institute of British Architects , and he was made an honorary member of the French Académie and a Chevalier of the Legion of Honor .
# text = A hundred years later , his counterpart is Frank O. Gehry .
# text = Even the staid American Institute of Architects , which had previously shunned Gehry in lieu of more mainstream practitioners , awarded him its top accolade , the AIA Gold Medal .
# text = No pair of architects could be more dissimilar than this distinctly odd couple , the proper High Society favorite of the Gilded Age and the untidy bohemian from Santa Monica .
# text = They were both late bloomers .
# text = Gehry was 48 when he gained national recognition .

# text = Until then , he had been running his own office in Los Angeles for almost twenty years , building shopping centers , suburban offices , department stores , and apartments in competent but unremarkable renditions of L.A. modern .

# text = The project that brought him to national attention was his own remodeled house : a nondescript bungalow encased in an unsettling Cubist composition of unpainted plywood , corrugated metal , and chain - link fencing .
# text = The odd shapes and unorthodox materials marked Gehry as a maverick .

# text = Unexpectedly , he attracted a broad range of commissions , not only residential clients , but also museums , public institutions , universities , corporations , and developers , and not only in the United States but around the world .
# text = Hunt was 43 when he came into his own .
# text = He had established an architectural practice in New York in 1855 , almost immediately on his return from the Ecole des Beaux-Arts .
# text = He was moderately successful , achieving local renown for the Tribune Building , an early New York skyscraper .
# text = Despite his Parisian background , Hunt worked in the prevalent Ruskinian Gothic style .
# text = For his next project , the Lenox Library , Hunt tried something different .

# text = He borrowed from the French Neo-Grec style , popularized by Labrouste in the Bibliothèque Sainte Genevi�ve , adding Renaissance details and his own characteristically vigorous surface modeling .
# text = The result was a startling departure from convention , a monochrome limestone block of imposing dignity .
# text = The 1880s was a decade of great prosperity , and newly wealthy New Yorkers eagerly sought out Hunt RSQUOs architectural blend of good taste and ostentatious display .
# text = He obliged them in a string of high - profile commissions : magnificent mansions along Fifth Avenue , country houses on Long Island , and palatial " cottages " in Newport , Rhode Island .
# text = Hunt died in 1895 , but in the last seven years of his life , he completed more than fifty projects .
# text = Biltmore House in Asheville , North Carolina , is a good example of his stylistic prowess .

# text = Hunt modeled the design of this 250 - room residence on the Château de Blois , whose style is not the severe Classicism of the Italian Renaissance favored by architects such as Charles McKim , but the more ornate and picturesque French Renaissance .

# text = To a modern visitor , the spires , turrets , and steep slate roofs of Biltmore recall Disneyland RSQUOs Sleeping Beauty Castle , which is not surprising since Disney also used a Loire Valley chateau ? the Château d?Ussé ? as his model .
# text = But the comparison does Hunt an injustice , for his design is neither prettified nor quaint .
# text = Vanderbilt was drawn to French chateaux , which Hunt showed him during a whirlwind European tour , since young George and his wealthy family imagined themselves American aristocrats .
# text = There are coats of arms bearing Vs all over the house .
# text = Hunt provides his client with an imagined regal setting , but deals with the past in his own peculiar way .

# text = Although he modeled the building on Blois , he makes no attempt to create a replica of the sixteenth - century chateau , but draws details from other buildings of the period and recombines them into an original whole .
# text = Nor does he try to create the illusion that this is a sixteenth - century building ? there is no artificial weathering , no aging effect no simulated historicism .
# text = The interior is modern , bright , and open .
# text = The focus of the main floor is a glass - roofed conservatory , a common nineteenth - century feature .
# text = The stonework of the house is impeccable , much crisper and more sharply defined than at Blois .
# text = Hunt was no antiquarian , and modern American technology abounds .
# text = The floors of fireproof hollow tile are supported by steel I-beams and the steep slate roofs by steel roof trusses .
# text = Cast iron replaces wrought iron and high - quality bricks , fired in the estate brickworks , back - up the limestone walls .
# text = Equally novel are the elevators and telephones , electrical lighting , hot and cold running water , and forced air central heating .
# text = There is no doubt that for Hunt , Biltmore is an up - to - the - minute modern building .
# text = That is part of its style , too .
# text = Like Hunt , Frank Gehry enlists novel materials in his buildings .
# text = The Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao , Spain , for example , is clad in titanium , previously used chiefly for building aircraft .
# text = The metallic walls curve , twist , and turn .
# text = One part of the building slides under an adjoining bridge ; another emerges from a reflecting pool .
# text = Bilbainos refer to the museum as the " artichoke , " which comes close to describing it , if you can imagine a gleaming , metallic artichoke more than two hundred feet high .
# text = The seeming disorder ? a chaotic collision of forms ? has no architectural precedent .
# text = This is not sculptural architecture , it is walk - in sculpture .
# text = " The plan is the generator " preached Le Corbusier , but with Gehry , the plan is the result .
# text = He appears to design from the outside in .
# text = The building as a composition comes first , the interior spaces follow .
# text = This implies that he shoehorns functions into the building , which is not the case .

# text = The Guggenheim has three distinct types of gallery spaces : traditional , skylit rooms for displaying its permanent collection of early Modernist art ; a long boat - like space for temporary installations ; and 11 smaller galleries , each with its own character , each dedicated to the works of a selected living artist .
# text = The artichoke accommodates them all .
# text = The building may appear offhanded , but there is nothing haphazard about the way it is organized .
# text = Gehry RSQUOs talent is his exceptional formal imagination ; his skill as an architect is to reconcile the forms he imagines with the functional demands of his client .
# text = And , of course , to find ways to build those forms .
# text = This is generally done without fuss .
# text = The titanium sheets simply follow the churning surfaces like shingles on a Shingle Style roof ; limestone is used in a similarly unaffected fashion , without articulated joints .
# text = Gehry shares a minimalist approach to details with the early architects of the International Style , but he deploys these details to different ends .
# text = By removing familiar elements such as coping strips , fascias , and trim , he accentuates the sculptural quality of his buildings .
# text = There are no roofs or walls or windows in the Guggenheim , there are only swirling and twisting planes of metal , stone , and glass .

# text = An architecture critic once described Gehry as " a smart man from Hollywood , " which nicely captures the architect RSQUOs blend of exuberant showmanship and canny behind - the - scenes savvy .
# text = Although sophisticated building techniques and innovative materials play a major role in Gehry RSQUOs buildings , like Hunt , he keeps technology off center stage .
# text = In that regard , he repudiates the mannered industrial style that pervades the work of many contemporary architects .
# text = Neither is he nostalgic about the past .
# text = Gehry rejects both the moralistic functionalism of the International Style and the traditions of Classicism .
# text = Architects have broken rules in the past , but rarely this unequivocally and totally .
# text = Gehry , like Hunt , has changed the course of architecture .
# text = That is , he has made us look at our surroundings in a different way .
# text = The world of Gehry RSQUOs buildings is , at first glance , an odd place .
# text = The line between order and disorder is a thin one , and it is difficult to know what is intended and what is accidental .
# text = But his colliding forms and agitated architecture are curiously unthreatening .
# text = This is the way we live today , Gehry seems to be saying , why not enjoy it ?

# text = To develop effective health policies , one must understand the existing health risks and disease burdens .
# text = On a worldwide scale , this is a tough challenge .

# text = The Global Burden of Disease Database , maintained by the World Health Organization ( WHO ) , collects data from countries around the world on risk factors such as tobacco , malnutrition , childhood abuse , unsafe sex , childbirth , and cholesterol levels , as well as on disease burdens , for example depression , blindness , and diarrhea .
# text = A large group of scientists from all over the world has developed a framework to analyze these data .
# text = To compare different risks or burdens , they calculate disability - adjusted life-years , or DALYs -- the number of healthy life years lost because of a particular disease or risk factor .

# text = Rodgers and colleagues used data from the WHO database for 26 risk factors and from 14 epidemiological subregions of the world to calculate the proportion of risk-factor - attributable disease burden in different population subgroups defined by age , sex , and exposure level .

# text = For being underweight in childhood , for example -- the leading risk factor for global loss of healthy life -- they found that only 35 % of the disease burden occurred in severely underweight children , the rest occurred in those only moderately underweight .

# text = The relative risks for the moderately underweight are much lower , but the number of children in that category is so large that the total attributable burden amounted to almost two-thirds of the total global burden of disease for that risk factor .

# text = The analysis confirms -- and extends to a global level -- previous research showing that many major health risks are important across the range of exposure levels , not just among individuals exposed to high levels of risk .
# text = It also points to risk factors that are particularly prevalent among specific populations and age groups , and for which highly targeted interventions could be effective .

# text = Despite numerous caveats and limitations of studies like this one , such analyses are essential aids in guiding the distribution of limited funds to lower the burden of life years lost to premature death and disability .

# text = By 1945 Siegel had become one of Las Vegas RSQUOs original visionaries , planning an opulent resort on the southern end of the LA Highway .
# text = When the Flamingo opened in December 1946 , it did so with Hollywood flair and the new Vegas flash .
# text = But the Mafia bosses who financed the operation were displeased with its performance ; Siegel was murdered in the summer of 1947 .
# text = Despite its initial failings , Siegel RSQUOs Flamingo survived him , as did mob infiltration of casinos .
# text = In fact , the Flamingo would launch over two decades of strong mob presence in Las Vegas .
# text = While the mob was running the casinos , promoters were busily selling Las Vegas as a glamorous Hollywood in the desert .
# text = From the mid-1940s to the mid-1960s , Las Vegas nurtured a growing sense that it was the " Entertainment Capital of the World . "
# text = Emerging stars , no longer content with playing small nightclubs , came to Las Vegas with dreams of making it big .
# text = Frank Sinatra , Wayne Newton , and Louis Prima each arrived with mediocre status and suddenly found themselves with names as big as the marquees on which they were written .

# text = The Rat Pack ? originally Frank Sinatra , Dean Martin , Sammy Davis Jr. , Peter Lawford , and Joey Bishop , all in town to film Ocean RSQUOs 11 ? landed at the Sands in January 1960 for a legendary stay .
# text = Other Hollywood stars came as well , simply because Las Vegas was the place to be .
# text = As a result , more casinos emerged along the Strip .

# text = The Thunderbird , Desert Inn , Sahara , Sands , and Riviera hotels were erected during this period , luring a curious clientele drawn by tales of all - night partying , exclusive entertainment , and cheap accommodations .
# text = There was no longer any question : when you wanted some unbridled adult fun , Las Vegas was the place to be .
# text = Organized crime was soon to have a formidable adversary in its bid to control Las Vegas ? corporate cash .

# text = Though Las Vegas had developed a powerful local economy , few major outside investments were made in the city , due primarily to mob infiltration and its inherent ties to illegal activities .
# text = That would change dramatically with the 1966 arrival of billionaire Howard Hughes .
# text = A legitimate businessman , Hughes was nonetheless eccentric and dramatic , a style suited to the Las Vegas ethos .
# text = True to the myth , the reclusive Hughes immediately cloistered himself in the Desert Inn RSQUOs penthouse .
# text = Several weeks later he was asked ? then ordered ? to vacate the room to make room for high rollers , whereupon he promptly bought the property and fired the management .
# text = Thus began Hughes ? legendary three - year , $ 300 - million Las Vegas buying spree .
# text = When it was over , Hughes owned six casinos , an airport , and an airline , along with numerous plots of land stretching from the Strip to the mountains .
# text = Hughes ? actions would have beneficial repercussions , both immediate and lasting .

# text = Because of the new legitimacy Las Vegas acquired from Hughes ? investments , established companies such as Hilton Hotels bought into the gaming business , and their influence helped draw a line in the desert sand between legitimate operations and mob casinos , where illegal skimming of profits was rampant .
# text = That , combined with the formation of the Nevada Gaming Control Board , would signal the beginning of the end for heavy mob influence in the city .
# text = Las Vegas with a Vision
# text = As corporations moved in and the mob was slowly pushed out , a new Las Vegas emerged .
# text = The legitimization of gambling led to its increased legalization across the US .
# text = What was once a sure thing became much more competitive .
# text = Casino operators had to reassess the nature of their business .
# text = The first to really do so was Steve Wynn , a Las Vegas resident and owner of the Golden Nugget .
# text = In the mid-1980s , Wynn began plans to reinvigorate Las Vegas with a new resort .
# text = He bought several Strip properties ? the Silver Slipper and Castaways among them ? and demolished them to make way for a new kind of resort ? Mirage ? which became an instant success .

# text = Wynn RSQUOs demolition of the existing properties started a trend that , more than any other , describes Las Vegas at the end of the 20th century : removal of old properties in exchange for the potential of new ones .
# text = Wynn RSQUOs casinos have also set new standards .
# text = They can no longer be just a box filled with gaming tables , restaurants , and a showroom .
# text = Excalibur , the MGM Grand , the Luxor , and New York - New York all followed Mirage RSQUOs lead during the 1990s , offering themed environments and attractions for families .

# text = As evidence of the " ever - faster " nature of the city , by the middle of the 1990s the new approach showed signs of backlash , with many visitors criticizing the mediocrity of the Las Vegas experience .
# text = The latest approach is perhaps the best of the post-mob era : the comprehensive resort .
# text = New resorts offer attractions and amenities modeled after those available in top resort cities worldwide , including luxurious spas , signature restaurants , and exclusive boutiques .
# text = Additionally , a handful of resorts ? such as the South - Seas themed Mandalay Bay , the Mirage , and the new Four Seasons ? are now catering exclusively to the luxury travel market .
# text = The crème de la crème of Las Vegas deluxe is Steve Wynn RSQUOs Bellagio .

# text = The world RSQUOs most expensive resort at $ 1.6 billion , the Bellagio RSQUOs amenities include 5 - star dining , Chanel - caliber boutiques , and a world - class collection of artistic masterworks .
# text = Perhaps more important , such high - end accommodations raise the standards of expectations back to the mythology of the Rat Pack era .
# text = Over 20,000 additional hotel rooms have been added in a few short years , including resorts in Summerlin and Lake Las Vegas .

# text = Recent business projections for Las Vegas predict challenges ; tourism revenues must increase substantially to sustain what is already built , while actual figures show visitation as steady or declining .
# text = The growth that has characterized Las Vegas for nearly a century may be facing a roadblock .
# text = Still , the future of Las Vegas is sure to be determined as much by the pioneering spirit that built the city as by anything else .
# text = With its new look and new aim , the prospects are good despite the warnings .
# text = Inevitably , some people will get burned in the process , but others will rise triumphantly from the fray to even greater successes .
# text = And that , more than anything , is the one constant that characterizes the past , present , and future of Las Vegas .

# text = It RSQUOs also a city of the imagination , reinvented and reappraised in the literature of its exiles .

# text = Prosperity has brought with it a new emphasis on historic preservation .

# text = The River Liffey flows from west to east through the center of the city to Dublin Bay .

# text = Buildings seem to transform themselves depending on the light ; Dublin under a lowering sky is a different place from Dublin in sunshine .
# text = Literature has always flourished in Dublin , the only city to have produced three Nobel Prize winners for literature ? Yeats , Shaw , and Beckett .

# text = The constantly crowded and busy Grafton street is the most visible center for shopping , but there are shops all over that carry an international array of goods as well as the Irish crafts and souvenirs you expect .

# text = Coffee has replaced the ubiquitous tea ? Dublin is now almost as much a coffee city as Vienna or Seattle .
# text = In a city of such human proportions it is not surprising that parks and gardens abound for recreation and relaxation .

# text = Hong Kong and Its People
# text = Exciting , mysterious , glamorous ? these words have described Hong Kong for at least a century .
# text = With its vibrant atmosphere and night - and - day activity it is an intoxicating place .
# text = Hong Kong is crowded ? it has one of the world RSQUOs greatest population densities .

# text = But it is also efficient , with one of the best transportation systems anywhere , and for such a crowded place , quiet ? you do n?t hear voices raised in anger , motorists sitting on their horns , or loud boomboxes .
# text = Shopping never ends ? there 's always another inviting spot just down the street .
# text = You RSQUOll find Hong Kong easy to get around , the people helpful , English spoken everywhere , and food that lives up to its reputation .
# text = On 1 July , 1997 the British Crown Colony of Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty as a Special Administrative Region of the People RSQUOs Republic of China .
# text = Today Hong Kong remains a capitalist enclave with its laws and rights intact , and China has promised that Hong Kong will continue in this fashion for at least 50 years .
# text = Beijing RSQUOs announced policy of maintaining Hong Kong RSQUOs prosperity and stability makes sense .
# text = Hong Kong has long been China RSQUOs handiest window on the West , and the city is unrivaled in its commercial know - how and managerial expertise .
# text = Around the time of the transition there was much speculation about how things would change .
# text = But in fact , once news of the handover vanished from the front pages , the people of Hong Kong returned to their usual topics of conversation : the economy and the price of housing .
# text = The impression of the visitor today will be that very little has changed .

# text = Establishments are no longer called " Royal , " Queen Elizabeth has vanished from the coinage , and the Union Jack has been replaced by the flag of China and the new Hong Kong flag with its bauhinia flower .
# text = But in fact , there have been changes , many of them due to economic progress , new construction , and other factors that influence cities all over the world .
# text = British social customs are still evident in the kind of polite service you get in hotels and in the long lines of people waiting for buses at rush hour .
# text = The British population has decreased ; today there are as many American and Australian ex-pats as there are British .
# text = Whole cities have been created in the New Territories , although the unimaginative architecture of these towns has been criticized .
# text = Of Hong Kong RSQUOs population , 98 percent are Chinese .
# text = The majority are Cantonese , born in Hong Kong , or from South China , but there are immigrants from all over China .
# text = The Chinese people have been described as hardworking and pragmatic , attitudes that have contributed to Hong Kong RSQUOs success .

# text = There are many stories of refugees who arrived with nothing in their pockets , set up a small sidewalk stall , worked diligently until they had their own store , and then expanded it into a modest chain .
# text = Old customs are still followed : Fate and luck are taken very seriously , and astrologers and fortune - tellers do a steady business .
# text = You RSQUOll also notice that gambling is a passion , whether it be cards , mah-jong , the lottery , or the horses .

# text = The crowded Kowloon peninsula and the booming New Territories on the mainland call for some serious sightseeing ; but we begin across Victoria Harbor on Hong Kong Island , where the city was first founded and which remains the center of government , business , and commerce .
# text = No matter how many tunnels and transit systems speed cross - harbor traffic , nothing matches the ride on the Star Ferry from Kowloon to the Central District across Victoria Harbor .

# text = As the double - decker boats get ready to leave the pier , bells ring , the gangplank is raised , deckhands in blue sailor suits man the hawsers , and a couple of hundred commuters begin a seven - minute sightseeing tour .
# text = The big green - and - white boat weaves its way through an ever - changing obstacle course of both large and small craft , and the soaring skyline of Hong Kong Island draws nearer .
